note: Life in the UK course, handbook-verified: original practice questions written from the 3rd edition handbook (Britizen PDF edition, page numbers of that edition). Every item cites chapter, section and page; facts changed since publication are worded 'According to the handbook' with a note. Only items with verification 'verified' and a page are imported.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, someone applying for permanent residence or citizenship agrees to respect the UK's:
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): Applicants accept the responsibilities of permanent residence and agree to respect the country's laws, values and traditions.

items.prompt: What does passing the Life in the UK test help to show, according to the handbook?
items.answer: That you are prepared to settle permanently in the UK
distractors: That you are qualified to work in the civil service
That you have lived in the UK for at least ten years
That you are entitled to free private healthcare
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The test is one part of showing that a person is ready to settle permanently in the UK.

items.prompt: The handbook says Britain is proud of its record of:
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The introduction says the UK is proud of how it has welcomed new migrants.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, what do new migrants add to the UK's national life?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The introduction says newcomers bring diversity and dynamism to national life.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The handbook describes applying to become a permanent resident or citizen as an important decision and commitment.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): Applying for permanent residence or citizenship is described as a significant decision and a commitment.

items.prompt: In which fields does the handbook say British people have been at the heart of world development?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The introduction names political, scientific, industrial and cultural development as areas where Britain's people have been central.

items.prompt: Besides preparing for the test, the handbook aims to help new residents:
items.answer: integrate into society and play a full role locally
distractors: find a job and open a bank account
choose a school and register with a doctor
learn to drive and buy a home
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The handbook is meant to help readers integrate and take a full part in their local community.

items.prompt: The handbook aims to give readers a broad general knowledge of the UK's:
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): One aim of the handbook is a broad general knowledge of British culture, laws and history.

items.prompt: How does the handbook describe Britain's history?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The opening of the handbook describes Britain's history as long and illustrious, and its society as modern and thriving.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, the questions in the Life in the UK test require an understanding of English at which level?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The test is written so that it needs English at ESOL Entry Level 3.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: According to the handbook, applications for permanent residence or citizenship can be submitted free of charge.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): A fee must be paid to submit an application, and the amount varies by application type.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, what decides which application form and evidence you must provide?
distractors: The date you passed the test
The region of the UK you live in
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The form and the supporting evidence depend on each applicant's own situation.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, from October 2013 people applying for settlement had to pass the Life in the UK test and also provide:
items.answer: evidence of their English at B1 level
distractors: proof that they own a home
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): From October 2013 the test had to be combined with evidence of English at level B1 on the Common European Framework of Reference.

items.prompt: Under the rules described for October 2013, which English skills had to be evidenced at B1 level?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The new requirement was for evidence of English speaking and listening skills at B1.

items.prompt: The handbook says level B1 of the Common European Framework of Reference is equivalent to:
distractors: level A2 of the same framework
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): B1 on the European framework is described as matching ESOL Entry Level 3.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, what has no place in British society?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The handbook states that extremism and intolerance have no place in British society.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, British values are protected by:
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The handbook says these principles come from the UK's history and traditions, and that law, custom and expectation protect them.

items.prompt: Where are the UK's fundamental values reflected, according to the handbook?
items.answer: In the responsibilities, rights and privileges of citizens and residents
distractors: Only in the words of the national anthem
In the rules of the Church of England
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The values show in the responsibilities, rights and privileges of British citizens and permanent residents.

items.prompt: Alongside democracy and the rule of law, which of these does the handbook list as a fundamental principle of British life?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): Participation in community life is one of the five fundamental principles listed.

items.prompt: Which of these is one of the freedoms the UK offers in return for residents' responsibilities?
distractors: Freedom to choose which laws apply
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): In return for residents' responsibilities, the UK offers several freedoms, including freedom from unfair discrimination.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Freedom of belief and religion is one of the freedoms the UK offers to people living here.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The freedoms offered by the UK include freedom of belief and religion.

items.prompt: In the citizenship pledge, to what do new citizens give their loyalty?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The pledge begins with a promise of loyalty to the United Kingdom.

items.prompt: In the citizenship pledge, new citizens promise to fulfil their:
items.answer: duties and obligations as British citizens
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The pledge ends with a promise to carry out one's duties and obligations as a British citizen.

items.prompt: In the citizenship pledge, new citizens promise to respect the UK's:
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): New citizens pledge loyalty to the UK and to respect its rights and freedoms.

items.prompt: Who does the handbook say should respect and support the fundamental values and principles of British society?
items.answer: All those living in the UK
distractors: Only people born in the UK
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The handbook expects everyone who lives in the UK to respect and support these values and principles.

items.prompt: How many questions are there in the Life in the UK test?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The test is made up of 24 questions on important aspects of life in the UK.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Everyone taking the Life in the UK test at the same session answers the same 24 questions.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): Each person at a test session gets a different set of 24 questions.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, apart from English, in which TWO languages can special arrangements be made to take the test?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The test is normally in English, but arrangements can be made to sit it in Welsh or Scottish Gaelic.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, why should you take the test only at a registered test centre?
items.answer: Only certificates from registered centres are accepted
distractors: Other centres charge much higher fees
Other centres only test in Welsh
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The UK Border Agency accepts certificates only from registered test centres.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, which people have separate arrangements for sitting the Life in the UK test?
items.answer: Residents of the Isle of Man or the Channel Islands
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): Residents of the Isle of Man and the Channel Islands have separate arrangements.

items.prompt: What must you take with you to the Life in the UK test?
items.answer: Identification and proof of your address
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): Candidates have to bring identification and proof of address to the test.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: If you arrive at the test without identification and proof of address, you will still be allowed to sit it.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): Without identification and proof of address you cannot take the test.

items.prompt: What does the handbook say about its 'Check that you understand' boxes?
items.answer: They are guidance, and knowing them alone is not enough to pass
distractors: They contain all the test questions
They are the only parts that are tested
They can be skipped because they are not tested
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): The boxes help identify key points, but you must understand the whole book to pass.

items.prompt: Where in the handbook are some key words and phrases explained?
items.answer: In the glossary at the back
distractors: In the index at the front
In the 'Check that you understand' boxes
In an appendix of test answers
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): A glossary at the back of the handbook lists helpful key words and phrases.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, which website explains ESOL courses and where to find one near you?
distractors: The Life in the UK test website
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): Gov.uk is named as the place to find out about ESOL courses in your area.

items.prompt: Test questions can be based on which parts of the handbook?
distractors: Only the chapters on government and law
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 1 (The values and principles of the UK): Questions may come from any part of the book, the introduction included.

items.prompt: What is the status of the rest of Ireland, the part that is not in the UK?
distractors: It is a British overseas territory
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): Northern Ireland is part of the UK, while the rest of Ireland is an independent country.

items.prompt: In the handbook, the words 'Britain' and 'British' are used to refer to:
distractors: only people born in the UK
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): The handbook uses 'Britain' and 'British' to mean everyone in the UK.

items.prompt: Where does the parliament that governs the UK sit?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): The UK is governed by the parliament at Westminster.

items.prompt: Which parts of the UK have their own parliament or assembly with devolved powers?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland each have their own parliament or assembly with powers in defined areas.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: British overseas territories such as St Helena are part of the UK.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 2 (What is the UK?): Overseas territories are linked to the UK but are not part of it.

items.prompt: Which report described the welfare state that Clement Attlee's new government promised to introduce?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Attlee became Prime Minister in 1945 promising to bring in the welfare state set out by William Beveridge.

items.prompt: What did the National Health Service, set up in 1948, guarantee?
items.answer: A minimum standard of health care for everyone, free when used
distractors: Free health care only for former soldiers and their families
Private health insurance paid for by every employer
Free hospital treatment only for children under 16
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The NHS promised everyone a basic level of health care with no charge at the point of use.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The national system of benefits introduced after 1945 was meant to protect people 'from the cradle to the grave'.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): A national 'social security' benefits system was created so that people would be looked after throughout their lives.

items.prompt: Which TWO were taken into public ownership by the Labour government after 1945?
items.answer: The railways and the coal mines
distractors: The coal mines and the newspapers
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The post-war Labour government nationalised the railways, coal mines and the gas, water and electricity supplies.

items.prompt: Which alliance did the UK join after the Second World War to resist the perceived threat from the Soviet Union?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The UK became a member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization, formed to resist a possible Soviet invasion.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: After the Second World War the UK relied entirely on the United States and never developed its own atomic bomb.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The handbook says the UK built its own atomic bomb in the post-war years and also joined NATO.

items.prompt: Which party was in government in Britain from 1951 to 1964?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Britain had Conservative governments between 1951 and 1964, a time of recovery and rising prosperity.

items.prompt: Which Prime Minister made the well-known 'wind of change' speech on independence for colonies?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Harold Macmillan, Conservative Prime Minister, spoke of a 'wind of change' bringing independence to countries of the Empire.

items.prompt: Which profession did Clement Attlee give up so that he could do social work in East London?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): After Oxford University Attlee became a barrister, but he left the law for social work in East London before becoming a Labour MP.

items.prompt: What position did Clement Attlee hold in Winston Churchill's wartime coalition government?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Attlee served as Churchill's deputy during the war and became Prime Minister when Labour won in 1945.

items.prompt: What was the official title of the 1942 Beveridge Report?
distractors: Health and Housing for the Nation
A National Plan for Full Employment
The Welfare of the British People
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The report commonly called the Beveridge Report was formally titled Social Insurance and Allied Services.

items.prompt: Which division in the school system, enforced by the Education Act 1944, still exists in most of Britain?
distractors: Between boys' schools and girls' schools
Between church schools and state schools
Between day schools and boarding schools
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Although education has changed a great deal since 1944, the split between primary and secondary schools introduced by the Butler Act largely remains.

items.prompt: What kind of work is Dylan Thomas's Under Milk Wood?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Under Milk Wood is a radio play by Dylan Thomas; it was first performed in 1954, after his death.

items.prompt: For whom did Dylan Thomas write the poem Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Dylan Thomas wrote the poem in 1952 for his father, who was dying.

items.prompt: Which city, where Dylan Thomas was born, has a statue of him and a centre named after him?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Swansea, Dylan Thomas's birthplace, remembers him with several memorials, including a statue and the Dylan Thomas Centre.

items.prompt: Facing labour shortages after 1945, the government encouraged workers from where to help rebuild Britain?
items.answer: Ireland and other parts of Europe
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): To help with post-war reconstruction, the government encouraged workers from Ireland and elsewhere in Europe to come to the UK.

items.prompt: In which year were people from the West Indies invited to come to work in Britain?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 1948 West Indians were also invited to come and work to help with post-war labour shortages.

items.prompt: Textile and engineering firms from which areas sent agents to India and Pakistan to recruit workers?
items.answer: The north of England and the Midlands
distractors: London and the south-east of England
Wales and the south-west of England
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In the 1950s firms in the north of England and the Midlands sent recruiters to India and Pakistan to find workers.

items.prompt: By what name is the 1960s often known in Britain?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The 1960s, a decade of great social change, was nicknamed 'the Swinging Sixties'.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Beatles and The Rolling Stones were two well-known pop groups of the 1960s.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The 1960s saw British fashion, cinema and pop music flourish, with The Beatles and The Rolling Stones among the best-known groups.

items.prompt: In the 1960s, laws on divorce and on which other matter were liberalised in England, Wales and Scotland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Social laws were relaxed in the 1960s, including those on divorce and on abortion in England, Wales and Scotland.

items.prompt: Which right did Parliament give women during the social changes of the 1960s?
distractors: The right to stand for Parliament
The right to sit in the House of Lords
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Parliament passed laws giving women equal pay and banning employers from discriminating against them because of their gender.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: In the 1960s many employers expected women to give up work once they married.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The handbook notes that women were often expected to leave work on marriage, before new laws improved their position.

items.prompt: Which supersonic passenger airliner did Britain develop together with France?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Britain and France jointly produced Concorde, the world's only supersonic commercial airliner.

items.prompt: Why did the number of migrants arriving from the West Indies and South Asia fall in the late 1960s?
items.answer: New laws restricted immigration to Britain
distractors: Economic growth kept workers at home
All vacancies in Britain had been filled
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The government passed new laws in the late 1960s limiting immigration, so the numbers arriving fell.

items.prompt: Under the immigration laws of the late 1960s, what were immigrants required to have?
items.answer: Close ties to Britain by birth or ancestry
distractors: A job offer approved by Parliament
A university degree from a British institution
The ability to speak both English and Welsh
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): After the late 1960s, people wishing to settle needed close ties to Britain by birth or ancestry.

items.prompt: In the early 1970s, 28,000 people of Indian descent expelled from which country were allowed into Britain?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Despite tighter immigration rules, Britain took in 28,000 people of Indian origin expelled from Uganda in the early 1970s.

items.prompt: Between which two cities did John Logie Baird make the first television broadcast in 1932?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Scotsman John Logie Baird developed television in the 1920s and in 1932 broadcast between London and Glasgow.

items.prompt: In which year did the first successful radar test take place?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Radar, developed by Sir Robert Watson-Watt, was first tested successfully in 1935.

items.prompt: Where is the radio telescope built by Sir Bernard Lovell, for many years the largest in the world?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Lovell's work with radar led to discoveries in astronomy; his radio telescope at Jodrell Bank in Cheshire still operates.

items.prompt: The Scottish physician John MacLeod was a co-discoverer of what?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): John MacLeod helped discover insulin, which is used to treat diabetes.

items.prompt: In which year was the structure of the DNA molecule discovered through work at British universities?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Research in London and Cambridge revealed the structure of DNA in 1953.

items.prompt: Which British scientist was among those awarded the Nobel Prize for discovering the structure of DNA?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Francis Crick, a Briton, shared the Nobel Prize for the discovery of DNA's structure.

items.prompt: In which year did Concorde begin carrying passengers?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Concorde first flew in 1969, entered passenger service in 1976 and was retired in 2003.

items.prompt: What was special about the Harrier jump jet, designed and developed in the UK?
distractors: It was the first jet airliner
It carried passengers faster than sound
It could take off and land on water
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Harrier jump jet was a British-designed aircraft able to take off vertically.

items.prompt: Who invented the cash-dispensing ATM, or 'cashpoint', in the 1960s?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): James Goodfellow invented the ATM in the 1960s.

items.prompt: Which TWO people pioneered IVF therapy in Britain?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): IVF treatment for infertility was pioneered by physiologist Sir Robert Edwards and gynaecologist Patrick Steptoe.

items.prompt: In which town was the world's first 'test-tube baby' born in 1978?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The first baby conceived by IVF was born in Oldham, Lancashire, in 1978.

items.prompt: Dolly the sheep was cloned in 1996 by a team led by Sir Ian Wilmot and which other British scientist?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Ian Wilmot and Keith Campbell led the team that first cloned a mammal, Dolly the sheep, in 1996.
items.notes: Handbook spells the name 'Wilmot' (usually written Wilmut).

items.prompt: Sir Peter Mansfield was co-inventor of which medical device?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Peter Mansfield co-invented magnetic resonance imaging, which gives detailed, non-invasive images of internal organs.

items.prompt: When did the post-war economic boom in Britain come to an end?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The handbook says the post-war boom ended in the late 1970s as prices rose sharply and the pound was unstable.

items.prompt: What were the 'balance of payments' problems of the 1970s?
items.answer: Imports were worth more than the money earned from exports
distractors: Exports were worth far more than imports
The pound was permanently fixed to the dollar
Wages rose much faster than prices
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Rising prices and an unstable pound meant Britain was paying more for imports than it received for its exports.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: In the 1970s many people argued that the trade unions had too little power.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Frequent strikes in the 1970s led many to argue that unions had become too powerful and were damaging the UK.

items.prompt: What happened to the Northern Ireland Parliament in 1972?
items.answer: It was suspended and the UK government ruled directly
distractors: It gained new powers over taxation
It moved from Belfast to Londonderry
It merged with the Irish Parliament
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Because of serious unrest, the Northern Ireland Parliament was suspended in 1972 and direct rule from the UK government followed.

items.prompt: About how many people lost their lives in the violence in Northern Ireland in the decades after 1969?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The handbook puts the number killed in Northern Ireland's violence since 1969 at around 3,000.

items.prompt: In which event did Mary Peters win an Olympic gold medal in 1972?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Mary Peters, an athlete from Northern Ireland, won Olympic gold in the pentathlon in 1972.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The athlete Mary Peters was born in Belfast.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Mary Peters was born in Manchester and moved to Northern Ireland as a child.

items.prompt: Margaret Thatcher's father was a grocer in which town?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Margaret Thatcher grew up in Grantham in Lincolnshire, where her father was a grocer.

items.prompt: What did Margaret Thatcher train as before her political career?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Thatcher trained in chemistry and law before being elected a Conservative MP in 1959.

items.prompt: In which year was Margaret Thatcher elected Leader of the Conservative Party?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Thatcher became Conservative leader, and so Leader of the Opposition, in 1975; she became Prime Minister in 1979.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: No Prime Minister of the 20th century served longer than Margaret Thatcher.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Thatcher held office from 1979 to 1990, longer than any other 20th-century Prime Minister.

items.prompt: Which United States President did Margaret Thatcher work closely with?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): As Prime Minister, Thatcher worked closely with President Ronald Reagan.

items.prompt: Margaret Thatcher was one of the first Western leaders to welcome changes in the leadership of which country, helping to end the Cold War?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Thatcher was quick to recognise new Soviet leadership, changes which ultimately helped bring the Cold War to a close.

items.prompt: How did the Thatcher government make structural changes to the economy?
distractors: By nationalising the railways and mines
By fixing the prices of all goods
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Conservative government of 1979-90 sold off nationalised industries and placed legal limits on trade union powers.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Conservative government led by Margaret Thatcher gave trade unions greater legal powers.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Thatcher's government did the opposite: it introduced legal controls on what trade unions could do.

items.prompt: What effect did deregulation in the 1980s have on the City of London?
items.answer: Its role as an international financial centre grew greatly
distractors: It lost most of its banks to other countries
It became the centre of British coal mining
It was placed under direct government control
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Deregulation greatly increased the City's importance as a world centre for investment, insurance and financial services.

items.prompt: Which TWO traditional industries declined during the 1980s?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): While the City grew, traditional industries like shipbuilding and coal mining declined under Thatcher.

items.prompt: Roald Dahl was born in Wales to parents of which nationality?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Roald Dahl was born in Wales; his parents were Norwegian.

items.prompt: Which of these is one of Roald Dahl's best-known books?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Dahl is best known for children's books such as Charlie and the Chocolate Factory and George's Marvellous Medicine.

items.prompt: Who led the Labour Party to victory in the 1997 general election?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Labour won in 1997 under Tony Blair, whose government created devolved bodies in Scotland and Wales.

items.prompt: Which TWO devolved bodies did the Blair government introduce?
items.answer: A Scottish Parliament and a Welsh Assembly
distractors: An English Parliament and a Scottish Parliament
A Welsh Assembly and an English Assembly
A Cornish Assembly and a London Parliament
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Labour government elected in 1997 set up a Scottish Parliament and a Welsh Assembly.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, how did the Welsh Assembly's powers compare with those of the Scottish Parliament when the two were created?
items.answer: It had fewer law-making powers but considerable control of public services
distractors: It had greater law-making powers than the Scottish Parliament
It had exactly the same powers as the Scottish Parliament
It had law-making powers but no say over public services
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Scottish Parliament was given substantial powers to make laws, while the Welsh Assembly had fewer but controlled many public services.
items.notes: changed since publication: the Welsh Assembly later gained full law-making powers (2011) and was renamed the Senedd / Welsh Parliament in 2020.

items.prompt: In which year was the Northern Ireland Assembly first elected?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Assembly was first elected in 1999, the year after the Good Friday Agreement was signed.

items.prompt: The Northern Ireland Assembly was suspended in 2002. When was it reinstated?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): After being suspended in 2002, the Assembly was not restored until 2007.

items.prompt: Who became Prime Minister after Tony Blair in 2007?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Gordon Brown took over from Tony Blair as Prime Minister in 2007.

items.prompt: After an Iraqi invasion in 1990, coalition forces with a leading British role liberated which country?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In the 1990s Britain played a leading part in the coalition that freed Kuwait after Iraq invaded it in 1990.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: British forces took a leading part in coalition action in the former Yugoslavia during the 1990s.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): As well as Kuwait, British forces took a leading part in the coalition involved in the former Yugoslavia.

items.prompt: In which year did British combat troops leave Iraq?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): British armed forces took part in operations in Iraq after 2000, and combat troops withdrew in 2009.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, the UN-mandated International Security Assistance Force (ISAF) in Afghanistan was a coalition of about how many nations?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The handbook says the UK served in Afghanistan within the 50-nation ISAF coalition, at the Afghan government's invitation.
items.notes: changed since publication: ISAF ended in December 2014 and UK combat operations in Afghanistan finished in 2014.

items.prompt: The general election of May 2010 was the first since when in which no party won an overall majority?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 2010 no single party won a majority, something that had last happened in the UK in February 1974.

items.prompt: Which TWO parties formed the coalition government in 2010?
items.answer: The Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats
distractors: Labour and the Scottish National Party
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): After the 2010 election the Conservatives and Liberal Democrats formed a coalition, with David Cameron as Prime Minister.

items.prompt: What was read at the coronation of William and Mary?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): A Declaration of Rights read at the coronation stopped the king from raising taxes or administering justice without Parliament.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Under the Bill of Rights of 1689, the king or queen had to be a Protestant.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Parliament decided who could be monarch and insisted that the king or queen must be Protestant.

items.prompt: Under the Bill of Rights, how often did a new Parliament originally have to be elected?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Elections had to be held at least every three years; this later became seven and is now five.

items.prompt: Today, what is the longest gap allowed between elections for a new Parliament?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The original three-year limit became seven years and is now five years.

items.prompt: After 1689, what did the monarch have to ask Parliament to renew every year?
items.answer: Funding for the army and the navy
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Each year the monarch needed Parliament's agreement to keep funding the army and navy.

items.prompt: By what name is the modern Conservative Party still sometimes known?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Whigs and Tories were the two main groups in Parliament, and Conservatives are still sometimes called Tories.

items.prompt: The laws passed after the Glorious Revolution mark the beginning of which system?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): These laws began constitutional monarchy: the monarch stayed important but could no longer force policies on Parliament.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: In the decades after William III, women who owned property were allowed to vote.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Only men owning property of a certain value could vote; no women had the vote at all.

items.prompt: What were constituencies controlled by a single wealthy family called?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): A constituency in the control of one rich family was called a pocket borough.

items.prompt: What were constituencies with hardly any voters called?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Constituencies with very few voters were known as rotten boroughs.

items.prompt: In which year did Jewish people settle in London for the first time since the Middle Ages?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 1656 Jewish people settled in London, the first to arrive since the Middle Ages.

items.prompt: Why did the Huguenots leave France?
items.answer: They were persecuted for their Protestant religion
distractors: They wanted to work in British factories
They were escaping a potato famine
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Huguenots were French Protestants who fled religious persecution between 1680 and 1720.

items.prompt: Which TWO kinds of work did many Huguenots do in Britain?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Many Huguenots were educated and skilled, working as scientists, in banking, or in weaving and other crafts.

items.prompt: Why was there uncertainty about who would succeed Queen Anne?
distractors: She had been forced to abdicate
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Queen Anne left no surviving children, which made the succession uncertain and led to the 1707 union.

items.prompt: What is the Act of Union of 1707 called in Scotland?
distractors: The Act for the Government of Scotland
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In Scotland the 1707 agreement that formed the Kingdom of Great Britain is known as the Treaty of Union.

items.prompt: Which church did Scotland keep after the union of 1707?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Scotland lost its independence but kept its own Presbyterian Church, as well as its legal and education systems.

items.prompt: Why did Parliament choose George I to be king in 1714?
items.answer: He was Anne's nearest Protestant relative
distractors: He had won the Battle of Culloden
He was the son of James II
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Parliament picked the German George I because he was Queen Anne's closest Protestant relative.

items.prompt: In 1714, who tried to make James II's son king instead of George I?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): An attempt by Scottish Jacobites to crown James II's son was quickly defeated.

items.prompt: Why did George I need to rely on his ministers?
items.answer: He did not speak very good English
distractors: He was too young to rule alone
He was a prisoner of Parliament
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): George I's weak English made him depend more on his ministers, leading to the role of Prime Minister.

items.prompt: During which years was Sir Robert Walpole Prime Minister?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Walpole, the first man called Prime Minister, held the post from 1721 to 1742.

items.prompt: In 1745, Bonnie Prince Charlie tried to replace which king?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The 1745 rising aimed to put a Stuart back on the throne in place of George II, George I's son.

items.prompt: How was Bonnie Prince Charlie related to James II?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Charles Edward Stuart, known as Bonnie Prince Charlie, was James II's grandson.

items.prompt: After Culloden, what did many clansmen become?
items.answer: Tenants who paid for the land they used
distractors: Members of the House of Lords
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The clans lost power after Culloden; chieftains favoured by the king became landlords and clansmen became paying tenants.

items.prompt: What were 'crofts' in the Scottish Highlands?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): During the Highland Clearances, landlords destroyed many crofts (small farms) to make room for sheep and cattle.

items.prompt: When did evictions during the Highland Clearances become very common?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Evictions from the land became very common in the early 1800s, and many Scots emigrated to North America.

items.prompt: In which languages did Robert Burns write?
items.answer: Scots, Scottish-flavoured English and standard English
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Burns wrote in the Scots language, in English mixed with Scottish words, and in standard English.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: As well as writing his own poems, Robert Burns changed or added lyrics to many traditional folk songs.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Burns revised a large number of traditional folk songs by altering or adding lyrics.

items.prompt: On what occasion is Auld Lang Syne usually sung?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Burns' song Auld Lang Syne is sung in the UK and elsewhere to celebrate the New Year, called Hogmanay in Scotland.

items.prompt: In which century did the Enlightenment take place?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Enlightenment was the development of new ideas in politics, philosophy and science during the 1700s.

items.prompt: Many of the great thinkers of the Enlightenment came from which country?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Many leading Enlightenment thinkers, such as Adam Smith and David Hume, were Scottish.

items.prompt: Which Enlightenment principle is still important in the UK today?
items.answer: Everyone may hold their own political and religious beliefs
distractors: The king rules by the will of God alone
Only property owners should have the vote
The state should choose people's religion
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): A key Enlightenment idea was that people may hold their own political and religious beliefs without the state dictating them.

items.prompt: Before the 18th century, what was the biggest source of employment in Britain?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Farming employed more people than anything else in Britain before the 1700s.

items.prompt: What were cottage industries?
items.answer: People working from home to make goods such as cloth and lace
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Before industrialisation many people produced goods like cloth and lace in their own homes.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Britain was the first country in the world to industrialise on a large scale.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Through the Industrial Revolution, Britain became the first country to industrialise widely.

items.prompt: Which TWO developments made the Industrial Revolution possible?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Industrial Revolution happened because of new machinery and the use of steam power.

items.prompt: Which TWO industries developed because of the Bessemer process?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Mass-produced steel from the Bessemer process led to the growth of shipbuilding and the railways.

items.prompt: What did Richard Arkwright originally train and work as?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Arkwright began as a barber who dyed hair and made wigs before moving into textiles.

items.prompt: Which machine did Richard Arkwright improve?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Arkwright improved the original carding machine and developed horse-driven spinning mills.

items.prompt: What is carding?
items.answer: Preparing fibres for spinning into yarn and fabric
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Carding prepares fibres so that they can be spun into yarn and made into fabric.

items.prompt: For what is Richard Arkwright particularly remembered?
items.answer: Running his factories efficiently and profitably
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Arkwright is best remembered for how efficiently and profitably he ran his factories.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: During the Industrial Revolution, laws protected employees from long hours and dangerous work.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): There were no laws protecting workers, who often worked long hours in dangerous conditions; children were treated the same as adults.

items.prompt: Who mapped the coast of Australia?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Captain James Cook mapped Australia's coast, and a few colonies were then set up there.

items.prompt: What was the East India Company originally set up to do?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The East India Company was created for trade but came to control large parts of India.

items.prompt: Which TWO goods did Britain import from North America and the West Indies?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Britain imported sugar and tobacco from North America and the West Indies, and textiles, tea and spices from India and Indonesia.

items.prompt: In which region of India did Sake Dean Mahomet grow up?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Mahomet, born in 1759, grew up in Bengal and later served in the Bengal army.

items.prompt: In which London street did Sake Dean Mahomet open his coffee house?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Mahomet opened the Hindoostane Coffee House, Britain's first curry house, in George Street in 1810.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: In the 18th century, slavery was legal within Britain itself.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Slavery was illegal inside Britain, although the overseas slave trade was a fully established industry.

items.prompt: From which region did most slaves transported on British ships come?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Slaves came mainly from West Africa and were taken to America and the Caribbean.

items.prompt: On which kinds of plantation were slaves made to work in America and the Caribbean?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Enslaved people were forced to work on tobacco and sugar plantations.

items.prompt: What were abolitionists?
distractors: Traders who bought and sold slaves
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Abolitionists, including William Wilberforce, wanted slavery abolished and turned public opinion against the trade.

items.prompt: How did the Royal Navy act against the slave trade?
items.answer: It stopped other countries' slave ships and freed the slaves
distractors: It carried slaves to the Caribbean
It ignored the trade at sea
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Royal Navy intercepted foreign slave ships, freed the slaves and punished the traders.

items.prompt: Why had many colonist families originally gone to North America?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Many colonists' families had moved to North America for religious freedom, and they valued ideas of liberty.

items.prompt: Which slogan did American colonists use against British taxes?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The colonists saw British taxes as an attack on their freedom and demanded representation in Parliament.

items.prompt: In which year did Britain recognise the independence of the American colonies?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): After the colonists defeated the British army, Britain accepted their independence in 1783.

items.prompt: In which year was there a revolution in France?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): France had a revolution in 1789, after which its new government quickly went to war with Britain.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Admiral Nelson survived the Battle of Trafalgar and later became Prime Minister.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Nelson led the British fleet at Trafalgar and died during the battle; it was Wellington who later became Prime Minister.

items.prompt: Where is Nelson's Column?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Nelson's Column in Trafalgar Square is a monument to Admiral Nelson.

items.prompt: Where can Nelson's ship, HMS Victory, be visited?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): HMS Victory, Nelson's flagship, is in Portsmouth.

items.prompt: What was the Duke of Wellington's nickname?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Wellington, who defeated Napoleon at Waterloo, was known as the Iron Duke.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: After his military career, the Duke of Wellington became Prime Minister.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Iron Duke went on to serve as Prime Minister.

items.prompt: Ireland became unified with England, Scotland and Wales in 1801 after which law?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Act of Union of 1800 joined Ireland with Great Britain from 1801.

items.prompt: What was the country created in 1801 called?
items.answer: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland
distractors: The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Union with Ireland in 1801 formed the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland.

items.prompt: How is the cross of St George described?
items.answer: A red cross on a white ground
distractors: A diagonal white cross on a blue ground
A diagonal red cross on a white ground
A white cross on a red ground
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): England's patron saint, St George, is represented by a red cross on a white ground.

items.prompt: In which year was the first Union Flag created from the flags of Scotland and England?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The first Union Flag was made in 1606, when Wales was already united with England.

items.prompt: Until which year did Queen Victoria reign?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Victoria reigned from 1837 until 1901, almost 64 years.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, which monarch had reigned longer than any other British monarch at the time of writing?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The handbook, written in 2013, describes Victoria's reign of almost 64 years as the longest of any British monarch.
items.notes: changed since publication: Queen Elizabeth II overtook Victoria's reign in September 2015.

items.prompt: Which group became increasingly significant within the UK during the Victorian Age?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In the Victorian Age the middle classes grew in importance and reformers worked to improve life for the poor.

items.prompt: Roughly how many British citizens left the UK between 1853 and 1913?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Many people were encouraged to settle overseas, and up to 13 million left between 1853 and 1913.

items.prompt: Between 1870 and 1914, which group of around 120,000 people came to Britain to escape persecution?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): About 120,000 Russian and Polish Jews arrived in this period, many settling in London's East End, Manchester and Leeds.

items.prompt: In which year were the Corn Laws repealed?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Repealing the Corn Laws in 1846 was an example of the government's free-trade policies.

items.prompt: What had the Corn Laws prevented?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Corn Laws blocked cheap grain imports; their repeal helped industry by making raw materials cheaper to import.

items.prompt: In 1847, what was the legal limit on the daily working hours of women and children?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): A law of 1847 restricted women and children to working 10 hours per day.

items.prompt: Which father and son pioneered the railway engine?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Just before Victoria's reign, George and Robert Stephenson pioneered the railway engine.

items.prompt: Where was Isambard Kingdom Brunel originally from?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The engineer Brunel came from Portsmouth in England.

items.prompt: At which London station does Brunel's Great Western Railway start?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Great Western Railway, Britain's first major railway, runs from Paddington to the south west, the West Midlands and Wales.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: In the 19th century, less than a tenth of all the iron, coal and cotton cloth made in the world came from the UK.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): British industry led the world: over half of all the iron, coal and cotton cloth produced globally came from the UK.

items.prompt: Besides manufacturing, the UK became a world centre for which services in the 19th century?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The UK became a centre for financial services such as insurance and banking.

items.prompt: Where was the Great Exhibition of 1851 held?
items.answer: In the Crystal Palace in Hyde Park
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Great Exhibition opened in 1851 in the Crystal Palace, a vast steel-and-glass building in Hyde Park.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Most of the objects shown at the Great Exhibition came from countries outside Britain.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Countries from around the world exhibited, but most of the objects were British-made.

items.prompt: In the Crimean War, Britain fought alongside Turkey and France against which country?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): From 1853 to 1856 Britain, Turkey and France fought Russia in the Crimean War.

items.prompt: The Crimean War was the first war to be what?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): News stories and photographs made the Crimean War the first war widely reported in the media.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: In the Crimean War, many soldiers died from illnesses caught in the hospitals rather than from their wounds.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Conditions were very poor, and disease picked up in hospitals killed many soldiers.

items.prompt: Which medal did Queen Victoria introduce during the Crimean War?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Victoria introduced the Victoria Cross, which honours acts of valour by soldiers.

items.prompt: In which country was Florence Nightingale born?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Florence Nightingale's parents were English, but she was born in Italy.

items.prompt: Where did Florence Nightingale train as a nurse?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): At 31 she trained as a nurse in Germany, then in 1854 went to military hospitals in Turkey.

items.prompt: In which year did Florence Nightingale set up her training school for nurses?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): She founded the Nightingale Training School at St Thomas' Hospital in 1860; it still exists.

items.prompt: Florence Nightingale is often regarded as the founder of what?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Because of her work and her training school, Nightingale is often seen as the founder of modern nursing.

items.prompt: In 19th-century Ireland, what proportion of the population still depended on farming?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Two-thirds of Irish people still made their living from farming, often on very small plots.

items.prompt: About how many people died in the Irish famine of the mid-19th century?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): When the potato crop failed, a million people died of disease and starvation and another million and a half emigrated.

items.prompt: Which Irish Nationalists favoured complete independence for Ireland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Within the 19th-century Irish Nationalist movement, the Fenians wanted full independence.

items.prompt: Who campaigned for 'Home Rule' for Ireland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Charles Stuart Parnell argued for Home Rule rather than full independence.

items.prompt: What did 'Home Rule' mean for Ireland?
items.answer: Staying in the UK but with its own parliament
distractors: Becoming fully independent of the UK
Being ruled from London with no Irish MPs
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Under Home Rule Ireland would remain part of the UK while having its own parliament.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Reform Act of 1832 abolished the old pocket and rotten boroughs.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The 1832 Act ended the pocket and rotten boroughs and gave more seats to towns and cities.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: After the Reform Act of 1832, members of the working class gained the right to vote.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Voting still depended on owning property, so working-class people still could not vote.

items.prompt: Which year's Reform Act created many more urban seats and lowered the property needed to vote?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Following the Chartists' campaign, the Reform Act of 1867 added urban seats and reduced the property qualification.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: After the Reform Act of 1867, most men were able to vote.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Even after 1867 most men still had no vote, and no women could vote.

items.prompt: What is universal suffrage?
items.answer: The right of every adult man and woman to vote
distractors: The right of property owners to vote
The right of all men only to vote
The right of anyone to stand for Parliament
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Universal suffrage means every adult man and woman has the vote; it came in the 20th century.

items.prompt: In which years were Acts passed letting married women hold on to their own earnings and property?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Acts passed in 1870 and 1882 allowed married women to retain their earnings and property.

items.prompt: What were women who campaigned for the vote in the late 19th and early 20th centuries known as?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Women campaigning for greater rights, especially the vote, formed the women's suffrage movement and were called suffragettes.

items.prompt: Which organisation did Emmeline Pankhurst set up in 1889?
distractors: The Women's Social and Political Union
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 1889 Pankhurst founded the Women's Franchise League to win local election votes for married women; the WSPU followed in 1903.

items.prompt: Which TWO forms of protest did the suffragettes use?
items.answer: Chaining themselves to railings and hunger strikes
distractors: Refusing to pay rent and boycotting tea
Burning ballot papers and leaving the country
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The WSPU used civil disobedience, including chaining themselves to railings, smashing windows, arson and hunger strikes.

items.prompt: In 1918, what right did women over 30 gain in addition to the vote?
items.answer: The right to stand for Parliament
distractors: The right to keep their own earnings
The right to join the army
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): From 1918 women over 30 could both vote and stand for Parliament.

items.prompt: Women over 30 were given the vote in 1918 partly in recognition of what?
items.answer: Their contribution to the First World War effort
distractors: Their support for the Boer War
Their work at the Great Exhibition
Their part in the Chartist petitions
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Votes for women over 30 in 1918 partly recognised what women had done for the war effort.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: At the end of the 19th century, the great majority of British people believed the Empire was a force for good.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Despite debate about the Empire's future, most British people saw it as a force for good in the world.

items.prompt: Who were the Boers?
items.answer: Settlers in South Africa from the Netherlands
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Boer War of 1899-1902 was fought in South Africa against settlers of Dutch origin.

items.prompt: In which country was Rudyard Kipling born?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Born in India in 1865, Kipling went on to live in India, the UK and the USA.

items.prompt: In which year was Rudyard Kipling awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Kipling won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1907.

items.prompt: Which of these books by Rudyard Kipling is still popular today?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Kipling's books, including the Just So Stories and The Jungle Book, remain popular.

items.prompt: Which TWO social measures were introduced in Britain in the early 20th century?
items.answer: Old-age pensions and free school meals
distractors: Free university tuition and old-age pensions
The National Health Service and free school meals
A national minimum wage and child benefit
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Reforms in the early 1900s included pensions for the elderly, free meals for schoolchildren and financial help for people out of work.

items.prompt: Which early 20th-century reform helped more people to enter public life?
items.answer: MPs were paid a salary for the first time
distractors: The voting age was lowered to 18
Women were allowed to become judges
The House of Lords was abolished
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Introducing a salary for MPs meant people without private wealth could more easily enter Parliament.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: In the early 20th century town planning rules were tightened to stop more slums being built.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Among the reforms of the period were stricter planning rules to prevent new slums, and laws to make workplaces safer.

items.prompt: Whose assassination on 28 June 1914 triggered the events that led to the First World War?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The killing of Archduke Franz Ferdinand in June 1914 triggered the First World War.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, which of these helped create the conditions for the First World War?
items.answer: Growing nationalism in many European states
distractors: A dispute over the Falkland Islands
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Besides the assassination, nationalism, militarism, imperialism and the split of Europe's powers into two camps set the scene for war.

items.prompt: Which TWO countries fought alongside Britain as Allied Powers in the First World War?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Britain's allies included France, Russia, Japan, Belgium and Serbia, later joined by others including the United States.

items.prompt: Approximately how many Indians fought on behalf of Britain in the First World War?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Over a million Indians fought for Britain in many countries, and about 40,000 of them were killed.

items.prompt: Which countries were the main Central Powers in the First World War?
items.answer: Germany, Austria-Hungary, the Ottoman Empire and Bulgaria
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Allies' main enemies were Germany, Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire, with Bulgaria joining them later.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: British casualties in the First World War numbered more than 2 million.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Millions were killed or wounded in the war, including over 2 million British casualties.

items.prompt: What did the British government promise Ireland in 1913?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 1913 Ireland was promised Home Rule: its own parliament while remaining in the UK.

items.prompt: What name is given to the 1916 uprising against the British in Dublin?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Irish Nationalists, unwilling to wait until after the First World War, rose against British rule in Dublin in 1916.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The leaders of the 1916 Easter Rising were pardoned and released by the British.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The leaders of the Easter Rising were executed under military law, and a guerrilla war followed.

items.prompt: What was the name of the southern part of Ireland after 1922?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The mainly Protestant six northern counties stayed in the UK, while the rest became the Irish Free State.

items.prompt: In which year did the Irish Free State become a republic?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Irish Free State, which governed itself, became a republic in 1949.

items.prompt: What is the conflict between those wanting full Irish independence and those loyal to the British government often called?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Disagreement over the partition of Ireland led to a terror campaign, and the conflict is often called 'the Troubles'.

items.prompt: In which year did the world enter the 'Great Depression'?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Great Depression began in 1929 and caused mass unemployment in some parts of the UK.

items.prompt: Which new industries developed in the UK during the depression of the 1930s?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Traditional heavy industries such as shipbuilding suffered, but car and aircraft manufacturing grew.

items.prompt: How did car ownership in the UK change between 1930 and 1939?
items.answer: It doubled from 1 million to 2 million
distractors: It halved from 2 million to 1 million
It tripled from 1 million to 3 million
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): As prices fell, people in work had more to spend, and the number of cars rose from one to two million.

items.prompt: Which TWO writers were prominent in Britain between the two world wars?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The inter-war years were a time of cultural blossoming, with Graham Greene and Evelyn Waugh among the leading writers.

items.prompt: Which economist published influential new theories of economics between the wars?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): John Maynard Keynes published important new economic theories in the inter-war period.

items.prompt: What did the BBC begin in 1936?
items.answer: The world's first regular television service
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 1936 the BBC launched the first regular television service anywhere in the world.

items.prompt: In which year did Adolf Hitler come to power in Germany?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Hitler took power in 1933, believing the post-1918 terms imposed on Germany were unfair.

items.prompt: Which event in 1939 led Britain and France to declare war on Germany?
distractors: The invasion of the Soviet Union
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Britain had hoped to avoid another war, but Hitler's attack on Poland in 1939 led Britain and France to declare war on Germany.

items.prompt: Which countries were the Axis powers at the start of the Second World War?
distractors: Germany, the Soviet Union and Japan
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): At first the Allies faced the Axis: fascist Germany and Italy, together with Imperial Japan.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Canada, Australia and New Zealand were among the main countries on the allied side at the start of the Second World War.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Besides the UK, France and Poland, the leading Allies included Canada, Australia, New Zealand and South Africa.

items.prompt: Which TWO countries did Hitler take control of after invading Poland and before advancing through France?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Hitler had already occupied Austria and invaded Czechoslovakia; after Poland he seized Belgium and the Netherlands, then moved through France in 1940.

items.prompt: Who became Prime Minister and Britain's war leader in 1940?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): As German forces swept through France in 1940, Winston Churchill became Prime Minister and led Britain in the war.

items.prompt: Which phrase arose from the 1940 evacuation of troops from France?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Although much was lost, the successful rescue from Dunkirk gave rise to the expression 'the Dunkirk spirit'.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Spitfire and the Hurricane, the RAF's key planes in the Battle of Britain, were designed and built in the United States.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Spitfire and the Hurricane were British-designed and British-built aircraft.

items.prompt: Which city was almost totally destroyed by German bombing during the Blitz?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Night-time bombing of British cities in the Blitz almost completely destroyed Coventry and badly damaged London's East End.

items.prompt: Which phrase is still used today when Britons unite to face hardship together?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Despite the bombing, a strong national spirit of resistance grew, remembered today as 'the Blitz spirit'.

items.prompt: Churchill lost the general election of 1945. In which year did he return as Prime Minister?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): After defeat in 1945, Churchill became Prime Minister again in 1951.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Winston Churchill was given a state funeral after his death in 1965.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Churchill remained an MP until 1964 and was honoured with a state funeral when he died in 1965.

items.prompt: Churchill's words 'Never in the field of human conflict was so much owed by so many to so few' were spoken during what?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Churchill made this speech to the House of Commons in 1940, during the Battle of Britain.

items.prompt: Churchill's 'We shall fight on the beaches' speech to the House of Commons followed which event?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Churchill gave the famous 'fight on the beaches' speech to the Commons after Dunkirk in 1940.

items.prompt: Where did the Japanese defeat the British before going on to occupy Burma and threaten India?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): While defending Britain, British forces also fought elsewhere; in Singapore they were defeated by the Japanese, who then occupied Burma.

items.prompt: What brought the United States into the Second World War?
items.answer: Japan's bombing of Pearl Harbour in December 1941
distractors: The German bombing of London in 1940
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The USA joined the war after Japan bombed the American naval base at Pearl Harbour in December 1941.

items.prompt: In 1941 Hitler launched history's largest invasion against which country?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Germany invaded the Soviet Union in 1941; its forces were eventually driven back with huge losses, a turning point in the war.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Allies won significant victories in North Africa and Italy during the Second World War.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Allies gradually gained the advantage, with important victories in North Africa and Italy.

items.prompt: When did the Allies comprehensively defeat Germany?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): After D-Day the Allies advanced through France into Germany, which was defeated in May 1945.

items.prompt: What ended the war against Japan in August 1945?
items.answer: US atom bombs dropped on Hiroshima and Nagasaki
distractors: A British invasion of the Japanese islands
A peace treaty signed in Singapore
The capture of Tokyo by Soviet troops
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The war with Japan ended when the United States used atom bombs on Hiroshima and Nagasaki.

items.prompt: Which scientist led the team that was the first to 'split the atom'?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Scientists led by Ernest Rutherford were the first to split the atom.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Manhattan Project, which developed the atomic bomb, was based in Britain.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Manhattan Project was in the United States; British scientists from Rutherford's team took part in it.

items.prompt: What was Alexander Fleming researching in 1928 when he discovered penicillin?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928 while he was studying the flu.

items.prompt: Which scientists turned penicillin into a usable drug?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Fleming's discovery was developed into a usable medicine by Florey and Chain, and it was mass-produced by the 1940s.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Penicillin is used today to treat viral infections.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Penicillin is still used to treat bacterial infections, not viral ones.

items.prompt: Which period of history ran from the Norman Conquest until about 1485?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The years after the Norman Conquest up to around 1485 are known as the Middle Ages.

items.prompt: What is another name for the Middle Ages?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Middle Ages are also called the medieval period.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Middle Ages were a time of almost constant war.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The medieval period saw nearly continuous warfare at home and abroad.

items.prompt: Which law of 1284 annexed Wales to the Crown of England?
distractors: The Act for the Government of Wales
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Edward I's Statute of Rhuddlan of 1284 joined Wales to the English Crown.

items.prompt: In which year did Edward I introduce the Statute of Rhuddlan?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Edward I annexed Wales to the Crown of England with the Statute of Rhuddlan in 1284.

items.prompt: By when had the last Welsh rebellions against English rule been defeated?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The final Welsh rebellions were crushed by the mid-1400s.

items.prompt: After the last Welsh rebellions were defeated, what was introduced in Wales?
items.answer: English laws and the English language
distractors: Norman French as the official language
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Once the rebellions ended, English law and the English language were brought into Wales.

items.prompt: What was the outcome of the Battle of Bannockburn?
items.answer: The Scots beat the English and Scotland stayed unconquered
distractors: The English conquered all of Scotland
Scotland and England were united under one king
The Vikings were driven out of Scotland
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): At Bannockburn in 1314 the Scots defeated the English, and Scotland was never conquered by England.

items.prompt: What was Ireland's status at the beginning of the Middle Ages?
distractors: Part of the Kingdom of England
A province of the Roman Empire
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Ireland was independent when the Middle Ages began.

items.prompt: Why did the English first go to Ireland in the Middle Ages?
items.answer: As troops to help the Irish king
distractors: As settlers escaping the Black Death
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): English soldiers first went to Ireland to help the Irish king and then stayed to found settlements.
