items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: In the Middle Ages, some important lords in parts of Ireland outside the Pale accepted the authority of the English king.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Besides ruling the Pale, the English king was accepted by some major lords elsewhere in Ireland.

items.prompt: What were the Crusades?
items.answer: Wars fought by European Christians to control the Holy Land
distractors: Wars between England and France over French land
Civil wars between the Houses of Lancaster and York
Campaigns to annex Wales to England
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Many English knights took part in the Crusades, fought by European Christians for the Holy Land.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: At the Battle of Agincourt, Henry V's English army greatly outnumbered the French.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Henry V's army was heavily outnumbered at Agincourt in 1415 but still defeated the French.

items.prompt: In which decade did the English leave France?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): After the long wars with France, the English left France in the 1450s.

items.prompt: What was the system of land ownership used by the Normans called?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Normans held land under the feudal system.

items.prompt: Under feudalism, what did the king receive in return for giving land to his lords?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The king granted land to his lords so that they would support him in war.

items.prompt: Under the feudal system, what did landowners have to provide?
items.answer: Men to serve in the army
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Landowners were obliged to send a set number of men to fight in the army.

items.prompt: In the Middle Ages, what were most peasants?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): A few peasants had their own land, but most of them were serfs.

items.prompt: Which of these was true of medieval serfs?
items.answer: They worked for their lord and were not free to leave
distractors: They owned large areas of land
They elected members of the House of Commons
They were paid high wages by the king
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Serfs grew food on a small patch of their lord's land, worked for him and were not free to leave.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The feudal system of land ownership also developed in southern Scotland.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The same feudal system grew up in the south of Scotland.

items.prompt: In the Middle Ages, who owned the land in the north of Scotland and in Ireland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In northern Scotland and Ireland land belonged to members of prominent families known as clans.

items.prompt: What was the Black Death probably a form of?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The disease that arrived in 1348 was probably a type of plague.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Black Death killed a much smaller share of the population in Scotland and Wales than in England.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): About a third of England's people died, and a similar share in Scotland and Wales.

items.prompt: After the Black Death, why was there less need to grow cereal crops?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): With far fewer people alive, less cereal was needed.

items.prompt: What did peasants begin to demand after the Black Death?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Labour shortages after the Black Death led peasants to ask for more pay.

items.prompt: After the Black Death, owners of large areas of land formed a new class later known as the:
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Large landowners became a new social class, later called the gentry.

items.prompt: What developed in the towns after the Black Death as a result of growing wealth?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Growing wealth in the towns produced a strong middle class.

items.prompt: How did the Black Death affect the English-controlled area of Ireland?
items.answer: It became smaller for a time
distractors: It grew to cover all of Ireland
It was given back to the Irish king
It was not affected at all
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Many people in the Pale died, so for a while the area under English control shrank.

items.prompt: The origins of Parliament can be traced to which body?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Parliament grew out of the council of advisers that served the king.

items.prompt: Which TWO groups were members of the medieval king's council of advisers?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The king's council included leading noblemen and the heads of the Church.

items.prompt: Which king was forced by his noblemen to agree to the Magna Carta?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 1215 King John's noblemen made him accept the Magna Carta.

items.prompt: What does the name 'Magna Carta' mean?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Magna Carta is Latin for the Great Charter.

items.prompt: The Magna Carta restricted the king's power to do what?
items.answer: Collect taxes or make and change laws
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The charter protected the nobles' rights and limited the king's power over taxes and laws.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Before 1215, there were few formal limits on the power of the king.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Until the Magna Carta of 1215, the king's power had few formal limits.

items.prompt: After the Magna Carta, whom would the king need to involve in his decisions?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): From then on the king had to include his noblemen in decision-making.

items.prompt: In medieval England, when in particular did the king call a parliament?
items.answer: When he needed to raise money
distractors: When a new bishop was chosen
When a battle had been lost
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Parliaments were summoned so the king could consult his nobles, especially to raise money.

items.prompt: Who sat in the medieval House of Lords?
items.answer: The nobility, great landowners and bishops
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The House of Lords was made up of nobles, great landowners and bishops.

items.prompt: Who were elected to sit in the medieval House of Commons?
items.answer: Knights and wealthy people from towns and cities
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Knights, usually smaller landowners, and rich townspeople were elected to the Commons.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: In the Middle Ages, most of the population could vote in elections to the House of Commons.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Only a small part of the population could take part in electing members of the Commons.

items.prompt: What were the three Houses of the medieval Scottish Parliament called?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Scotland's Parliament had three Houses, known as Estates.

items.prompt: Besides the lords, which TWO groups made up the Estates of the medieval Scottish Parliament?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The three Estates were the lords, the commons and the clergy.

items.prompt: Which legal principle began to be established in the Middle Ages?
items.answer: That judges are independent of the government
distractors: That the king chooses every jury
That only bishops may judge cases
That judges are elected by the people
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The idea of judicial independence from government started to take hold in this period.

items.prompt: How did the legal system in medieval Scotland differ from that in England?
items.answer: Scottish laws were codified, or written down
distractors: Scotland had no courts at all
Scottish laws were made by the clergy alone
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): English judges built common law from precedent, while in Scotland laws were written down.

items.prompt: After the Norman Conquest, which language did the king and his noblemen speak?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Norman king and nobles spoke Norman French while peasants kept speaking Anglo-Saxon.

items.prompt: Which TWO modern English words are based on Norman French words?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): 'Park' and 'beauty' come from Norman French; 'apple', 'cow' and 'summer' come from Anglo-Saxon.

items.prompt: Which of these English words is based on an Anglo-Saxon word?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): 'Summer' is one of the handbook's examples of words with Anglo-Saxon origins.

items.prompt: 'Demand' comes from French. Which word with a similar meaning does the handbook say comes from Anglo-Saxon?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The handbook pairs French 'demand' with Anglo-Saxon 'ask' as words of similar meaning.

items.prompt: By about which year were official documents in England being written in English?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): By 1400 official documents in England were written in English.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: By 1400, Norman French was still the preferred language of the English royal court and Parliament.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): By 1400 English, not French, was the preferred language at the royal court and in Parliament.

items.prompt: What are the characters in The Canterbury Tales doing?
items.answer: Going on a pilgrimage and telling stories
distractors: Fighting in the Hundred Years War
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Chaucer's poems describe pilgrims travelling to Canterbury and the tales they tell each other on the way.

items.prompt: In which language did Geoffrey Chaucer write The Canterbury Tales?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Chaucer wrote his series of poems in English.

items.prompt: When did Geoffrey Chaucer write The Canterbury Tales?
items.answer: In the years leading up to 1400
distractors: During the reign of Henry VIII
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Chaucer wrote the poems in the period before 1400.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Canterbury Tales was one of the first books printed by William Caxton.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Caxton, who first printed books on a press in England, printed The Canterbury Tales among his earliest titles.

items.prompt: In medieval Scotland, besides Gaelic, which language developed and was used by a number of poets?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Many Scots kept speaking Gaelic, and the Scots language also developed and was used by poets.

items.prompt: Who wrote The Bruce, a poem about the Battle of Bannockburn?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): John Barbour, writing in Scots, composed The Bruce about Bannockburn.

items.prompt: Which medieval castle does the handbook mention as still being in use today?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Many medieval castles are ruins, but some, such as Windsor and Edinburgh, are still used.

items.prompt: Why were castles built in many places in medieval Britain and Ireland?
distractors: As hospitals during the Black Death
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Castles were built across Britain and Ireland, partly to defend the land.

items.prompt: What did the stained glass windows in medieval cathedrals tell stories about?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Several cathedrals had stained glass windows showing stories from the Bible and of Christian saints.

items.prompt: York Minster is famous for its:
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The handbook gives the glass in York Minster as a famous example of medieval stained glass.

items.prompt: Which product became a very important English export in the Middle Ages?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): England was a major trading nation and English wool was a very important export.

items.prompt: Skilled weavers who came to work in medieval England came from which country?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): People with special skills came to England, including weavers from France.

items.prompt: From which country did canal builders come to work in medieval England?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Canal builders from Holland were among the skilled workers who came to England.

items.prompt: From which country did glass manufacturers come to work in medieval England?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Italian glass manufacturers were among the skilled workers who came to England.

items.prompt: In which year did the Wars of the Roses begin?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The civil war known as the Wars of the Roses started in 1455.

items.prompt: What was the Wars of the Roses fought to decide?
items.answer: Who should be king of England
distractors: Who owned the land in Ireland
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Wars of the Roses was a civil war over who should be king of England.

items.prompt: Who led the House of Lancaster and became king after the Battle of Bosworth Field?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Henry Tudor, leader of the Lancastrians, became King Henry VII after Bosworth.

items.prompt: Whom did Henry VII marry, uniting the Houses of Lancaster and York?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Henry VII married Elizabeth of York, King Richard's niece, joining the two families.

items.prompt: How was Elizabeth of York related to King Richard III?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Henry VII's wife, Elizabeth of York, was Richard III's niece.

items.prompt: Who became the first Tudor king?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Henry VII, formerly Henry Tudor, was the first Tudor king.

items.prompt: Henry VII was careful with money. What did this allow him to do?
items.answer: Build up the monarchy's financial reserves
distractors: Pay for a long war against Spain
Build the first Tower of London
Fund Drake's voyage around the world
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Henry VII was thrifty, so he was able to build up the Crown's financial reserves.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Henry VIII reversed his father's policy and handed more power back to the nobles.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Henry VIII carried on his father's policy of centralising power rather than reversing it.

items.prompt: How many times did Henry VIII marry?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Henry VIII is famous for having six wives as well as for breaking with the Church of Rome.

items.prompt: Which child of Henry VIII and Catherine of Aragon survived?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Henry and Catherine of Aragon had several children, but Mary was the only one to survive.

items.prompt: Where was Anne Boleyn executed?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Anne Boleyn, accused of taking lovers, was put to death at the Tower of London.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Jane Seymour died shortly after giving birth to Henry VIII's son.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Jane Seymour gave Henry his longed-for son, Edward, but died soon after the birth.

items.prompt: Which wife of Henry VIII was a German princess, married for political reasons?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Anne of Cleves came from Germany; Henry married her for political reasons and soon divorced her.

items.prompt: In Henry VIII's new Church of England, who had the power to appoint bishops?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In the Church of England the king, and no longer the Pope, appointed bishops and decided how people should worship.

items.prompt: What was the Reformation?
items.answer: A movement against the Pope's authority and Catholic practices
distractors: A campaign to give all adult men the vote
A movement to restore Catholicism in England
A plan to unite England and Scotland
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Reformation spread across Europe as a challenge to the Pope's authority and to Roman Catholic ideas and practices.

items.prompt: Instead of Latin, in which language did Protestants read the Bible?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Protestants read the Bible in their own languages rather than in Latin.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Protestants at the time of the Reformation prayed to saints and at shrines.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Protestants rejected praying to saints and at shrines.

items.prompt: What led to rebellion by Irish chieftains in the Tudor period?
items.answer: English attempts to impose Protestantism and English land laws
distractors: The repeal of the Corn Laws in Ireland
The failure of the Irish potato crop
The creation of the Union Flag
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): English efforts to force Protestantism on Ireland, together with English rules on inheriting land, provoked rebellion and brutal fighting.

items.prompt: After Wales was formally united with England under Henry VIII, where did the Welsh send representatives?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Under the Act for the Government of Wales, Welsh representatives sat in the House of Commons and Welsh law was reformed.

items.prompt: Which son of Henry VIII was strongly Protestant?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Henry VIII's successor was his son Edward VI, a firm Protestant.

items.prompt: How old was Edward VI when he died?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Edward VI died aged 15, having reigned for just over six years.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Elizabeth I questioned people closely about their real religious beliefs.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Elizabeth required church attendance and set rules for services, but she did not enquire into what people really believed.

items.prompt: How did Elizabeth I avoid serious religious conflict in England?
items.answer: By balancing Catholic and more extreme Protestant views
distractors: By making Catholicism the official religion
By abolishing the Church of England
By letting people stop attending church
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Elizabeth found a middle way between Catholics and the more extreme Protestants, which kept religious peace in England.

items.prompt: Why did Spain send the Armada against England in 1588?
items.answer: To conquer England and restore Catholicism
distractors: To claim Ireland for the Spanish crown
To protect Spanish trade with India
To support Parliament against the king
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Armada was a large Spanish fleet sent to conquer England and bring back Catholicism; its defeat made Elizabeth very popular.

items.prompt: In which year did the Scottish Parliament abolish the Pope's authority in Scotland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In 1560 the mainly Protestant Scottish Parliament ended papal authority and made Roman Catholic services illegal.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Unlike the Church of England, the Protestant Church of Scotland established in the 16th century was not a state Church.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): A Protestant Church of Scotland was set up, but unlike in England it was not a state Church.

items.prompt: How old was Mary Stuart when she became Queen of Scotland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Mary's father died when she was only a week old, making her queen as a baby.

items.prompt: Why did Mary, Queen of Scots flee to England?
items.answer: She was suspected of involvement in her husband's murder
distractors: Scotland had been invaded by Spain
She had lost the Battle of Culloden
She had been defeated by Cromwell
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): After her husband was murdered and suspicion fell on her, Mary escaped to England.

items.prompt: To whom did Mary, Queen of Scots give her throne?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Mary handed the Scottish throne to her son James VI, who was a Protestant.

items.prompt: How was Mary, Queen of Scots related to Elizabeth I?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Mary, Elizabeth I's cousin, hoped Elizabeth would help her, but Elizabeth distrusted her.

items.prompt: For how long did Elizabeth I keep Mary, Queen of Scots a prisoner?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Suspecting that Mary wanted the English throne, Elizabeth held her captive for 20 years.

items.prompt: Which commander in the defeat of the Spanish Armada is seen as a founding figure of English naval tradition?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Sir Francis Drake helped defeat the Armada and is regarded as a founding figure of English naval tradition.

items.prompt: The Golden Hind was one of the first ships to do what?

items.prompt: In Elizabeth I's time, where did English settlers first begin to establish colonies?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): English settlers began colonising America's east coast during Elizabeth I's reign.

items.prompt: Besides writing plays and poems, what else was William Shakespeare?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Shakespeare was both a playwright and an actor, as well as a poet.

items.prompt: Which TWO are among Shakespeare's most famous plays?
items.answer: A Midsummer Night's Dream and Macbeth
distractors: Romeo and Juliet and The Jungle Book
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Among Shakespeare's best-known plays are Hamlet, Macbeth, Romeo and Juliet and A Midsummer Night's Dream.

items.prompt: Shakespeare was one of the first writers to portray which people?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Although he wrote about historical events, Shakespeare did not limit himself to royalty and was an early portrayer of ordinary English people.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Shakespeare invented many words that are still in common use today.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Shakespeare greatly influenced the English language and created many words still used now.

items.prompt: 'Once more unto the breach' is a line from which Shakespeare play?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): This often-quoted line comes from Shakespeare's Henry V.

items.prompt: In which Shakespeare play does the line 'A rose by any other name' appear?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): 'A rose by any other name' is a quotation from Romeo and Juliet.

items.prompt: 'All the world's a stage' comes from which Shakespeare play?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The line 'All the world's a stage' is from As You Like It.

items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The phrase comes from Shakespeare's Sonnet 18.

items.prompt: What is the Globe Theatre in London?
items.answer: A modern copy of the kind of theatre where Shakespeare's plays were first staged
distractors: The original theatre Shakespeare built, still unchanged
A theatre designed by Sir Christopher Wren after 1666
The building where the Great Exhibition of 1851 was held

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Elizabeth I married and had children, but none of them outlived her.

items.prompt: By what other name is the King James Version of the Bible known?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The English Bible translated in King James's reign is called the King James Version or the Authorised Version.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The King James Bible was the first Bible ever translated into English.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The King James Version was not the first English Bible, but it is still used in many Protestant churches.

items.prompt: What title did Henry VIII take in relation to Ireland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Henry VIII extended English authority over Ireland and called himself King of Ireland.

items.prompt: In Tudor Ireland, whose instructions were local leaders expected to follow?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): English laws were brought in and local leaders had to obey the Lord Lieutenants based in Dublin.

items.prompt: Many of the new settlers in the Ulster plantations came from which area?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Many Ulster settlers came from south-west Scotland, while other land was handed to London-based companies.

items.prompt: Which monarch was very skilled at managing Parliament?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Elizabeth I balanced her own wishes against those of both Houses of Parliament, unlike James I and Charles I.

items.prompt: For how many years did Charles I raise money without Parliament's approval?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Charles I governed without Parliament for 11 years until trouble in Scotland forced him to recall it.

items.prompt: Why did Charles I's revised Prayer Book cause serious unrest in Scotland?
items.answer: He tried to impose it on the Presbyterian Church there

It banned the Bible in English
It made the Pope head of the Church
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Charles wanted more ceremony in worship and tried to force his revised Prayer Book on Scotland's Presbyterian Church, provoking unrest.

items.prompt: In which year did Charles I recall Parliament to ask for funds?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Needing money to fight a Scottish army, Charles recalled Parliament in 1640.

items.prompt: Who were the Puritans?
items.answer: Protestants who wanted strict and simple religious worship
distractors: Supporters of James II in exile
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Puritans were Protestants who favoured strict, plain doctrine and worship; many sat in Parliament and opposed Charles I's church reforms.

items.prompt: Why did Roman Catholics in Ireland rebel against the government in the 1640s?
items.answer: They feared the growing power of the Puritans
distractors: Henry VIII had just taken the Irish crown
The Corn Laws had been introduced
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): A rebellion broke out in Ireland because Catholics there were afraid of the rising influence of the Puritans.

items.prompt: How many parliamentary leaders did Charles I try to arrest in the House of Commons?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Charles I entered the Commons to arrest five leaders, but the men had been warned and stayed away.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Several monarchs have entered the House of Commons since Charles I's attempted arrests.

items.prompt: In which year did the English Civil War begin?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): War between the king and Parliament could no longer be avoided and broke out in 1642.

items.prompt: What were supporters of Parliament called in the English Civil War?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The country divided into the king's supporters, the Cavaliers, and Parliament's supporters, the Roundheads.

items.prompt: After the execution of Charles I, what was the English republic called?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): England became a republic without a monarch, known as the Commonwealth.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Oliver Cromwell is still a controversial figure in Ireland because of the violence of his campaign there.

items.prompt: After Charles I's execution, whom did the Scots declare to be king?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Scots, who had opposed the execution, proclaimed Charles I's son, Charles II, as their king.

items.prompt: At which TWO battles did Cromwell defeat the Scottish army led by Charles II?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Charles II, crowned in Scotland, led an army into England but was beaten by Cromwell at Dunbar and Worcester.

items.prompt: Where did Charles II famously hide after the Battle of Worcester?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Charles II escaped from Worcester, on one occasion hiding in an oak tree, and later fled to Europe.

items.prompt: In which year did Oliver Cromwell die?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Cromwell ruled as Lord Protector until his death in 1658.

items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Richard Cromwell succeeded his father but could not control the army or the government.

items.prompt: From which country did Charles II return from exile in 1660?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): In May 1660 Charles II was invited by Parliament to return from the Netherlands, where he had been in exile.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: After the Restoration, Roman Catholics and Puritans alike were excluded from power.

items.prompt: Who wrote a diary describing the plague and the Great Fire of London?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Samuel Pepys described these events in his diary, which was published later and is still read.

items.prompt: What does 'habeas corpus' mean?

distractors: The king can do no wrong

items.prompt: In which year did the Habeas Corpus Act become law?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Habeas Corpus Act of 1679 ensured no one could be imprisoned unlawfully, and it still matters today.

items.prompt: Which early member of the Royal Society correctly predicted the return of a comet?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Sir Edmund Halley, an early Royal Society member, predicted the comet's return; it now bears his name.

items.prompt: In which county was Isaac Newton born?

items.answer: It is composed of the colours of the rainbow
distractors: It travels more slowly than sound
It is produced only by the Sun
It contains no colours at all

items.prompt: James II went against an Act of Parliament by allowing Roman Catholics to do what?
distractors: Sit on the throne of Scotland

items.prompt: What made people fear that the monarch after James II would not be Protestant?
distractors: Parliament abolished the Church of England
William of Orange became a Catholic
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): James's heirs were two Protestant daughters until his wife gave birth to a son, who would take precedence.

items.prompt: William of Orange was the Protestant ruler of which country?

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: After the Glorious Revolution, William ruled jointly with Mary.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): William took the throne and shared rule with his wife Mary.

items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): James II landed in Ireland backed by a French army but was beaten at the Boyne.

items.prompt: After William re-conquered Ireland, what happened to Irish Catholics?

They were allowed to be army officers

items.prompt: For much of the Stone Age, how was Britain connected to the continent?

items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Hunter-gatherers moved with the herds of deer and horses they hunted.

items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Stonehenge was probably a place where people gathered for seasonal ceremonies.

items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The well-preserved village of Skara Brae shows how people lived late in the Stone Age.

items.prompt: About how long ago did people in Britain learn to make bronze?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Bronze Age began around 4,000 years ago.

items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Bronze Age people lived in roundhouses.

items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Skilled Bronze Age metalworkers made tools, ornaments and weapons in bronze and gold.

items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): After the Bronze Age came the Iron Age, when people learned to work iron.

items.prompt: What were Iron Age hill forts?
items.answer: Defended sites where people sometimes lived

items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): Most Iron Age people farmed, worked at crafts or were warriors.

items.explanation: Handbook ch. 3 (A long and illustrious history): The Anglo-Saxon kingdoms were mainly in England; much of Wales and Scotland stayed free.
