Every candidate who gets over 10% of the votes
The candidate with the longest party membership
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): In each constituency the candidate with the largest number of votes wins the seat.

items.prompt: Where can you find contact details for your elected representatives?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Contact details for representatives and their parties are available from local libraries and the Parliament website.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, Britain's tradition of protecting individual rights has its roots in which TWO of these?
items.answer: Magna Carta and the Bill of Rights of 1689
distractors: The Treaty of Rome and the Act of Union
The Domesday Book and the Beveridge Report
The Reform Act and the Education Act
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): British rights are traced back to Magna Carta, the Habeas Corpus Act and the 1689 Bill of Rights.

items.prompt: Who played an important part in drafting the European Convention on Human Rights?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): British diplomats and lawyers had a key role in writing the Convention.

items.prompt: In which year did the UK sign the European Convention on Human Rights, as one of the first countries to do so?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The UK was among the first signatories of the Convention in 1950.

items.prompt: Which of these is one of the principles in the European Convention on Human Rights?
items.answer: The right to a fair trial
distractors: The right to a free house
The right to a job for life
The right to free university education
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The Convention includes the right to a fair trial, among other principles.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The European Convention on Human Rights prohibits slavery and forced labour.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Prohibition of slavery and forced labour is one of the Convention's principles.

items.prompt: Which of these freedoms is included in the European Convention on Human Rights?
items.answer: Freedom of thought, conscience and religion
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The Convention protects freedom of thought, conscience and religion, and freedom of expression.

items.prompt: Under the Human Rights Act 1998, who must follow the principles of the European Convention on Human Rights?
items.answer: The government, public bodies and the courts
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The Act requires the government, public bodies and courts to follow the Convention.

items.prompt: UK law protects people from unfair treatment at work because of which of these?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The grounds covered include marital status, as well as age, disability, sex, race, religion or belief, sexuality, and pregnancy and maternity.

items.prompt: In England and Wales, which organisation can give information if you face discrimination?
items.answer: The Equality and Human Rights Commission
distractors: The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The Equality and Human Rights Commission covers England and Wales.

items.prompt: Which body deals with equality issues in Northern Ireland?
items.answer: The Equality Commission for Northern Ireland
distractors: The Electoral Office for Northern Ireland
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Northern Ireland has its own Equality Commission, and also a Human Rights Commission.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Someone who is violent towards their partner can be prosecuted only if the couple are married.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Violence towards a partner is a serious crime whether the couple are married or living together, and whether the abuser is a man or woman.

items.prompt: What are the safe places where people escaping domestic violence can stay called?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): In some areas there are refuges or shelters for people facing domestic violence.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The National Domestic Violence Freephone Helpline can only be called during office hours.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The freephone helpline runs 24 hours a day, so it can be called at any time.

items.prompt: What other names are used for female genital mutilation (FGM)?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): FGM is also referred to as cutting or female circumcision.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: It is a crime to take a girl or woman out of the UK so that FGM can be carried out.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Both carrying out FGM and taking someone overseas for it are crimes.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Arranged marriages where both people agree to marry are acceptable in the UK.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Marriage requires full and free consent; arranged marriages with the agreement of both are acceptable.

items.prompt: What makes a marriage a forced marriage?
items.answer: One or both people do not or cannot consent to it
distractors: The couple's families arranged the introduction
The wedding takes place outside the UK
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): A forced marriage is one in which one or both parties do not or cannot consent.

items.prompt: In which year were Forced Marriage Protection Orders introduced in England, Wales and Northern Ireland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The orders came in during 2008 under the Forced Marriage (Civil Protection) Act 2007.

items.prompt: When were Protection Orders similar to Forced Marriage Protection Orders introduced in Scotland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Scotland introduced similar orders in November 2011.

items.prompt: What is the maximum prison sentence for breaching a Forced Marriage Protection Order?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Breaching an order is contempt of court and can lead to up to two years in prison.

items.prompt: Who can apply for a Forced Marriage Protection Order?
items.answer: A potential victim or someone acting for them
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The potential victim, or a person acting on their behalf, may apply.

items.prompt: What is money raised from income tax used for?
items.answer: Government services such as roads, education, police and the armed forces
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Income tax funds public services like roads, schools, the police and the armed forces.

items.prompt: What is the system called in which employers deduct income tax from wages and pay it to HMRC?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Under PAYE the employer takes the right amount of tax from pay and sends it to HMRC.

items.prompt: How do employees usually pay their National Insurance Contributions?
items.answer: Their employer deducts them from their pay
distractors: They pay them in cash at a post office
They pay them once a year through the council
They do not pay any; only the self-employed do
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Employers deduct employees' contributions from pay, while the self-employed pay their own.

items.prompt: What may happen to someone who does not pay enough National Insurance Contributions?
items.answer: They may lose entitlement to some contributory benefits, such as Jobseeker's Allowance or the full state pension
distractors: They will lose the right to vote
They will be refused a driving licence
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Insufficient contributions can mean losing entitlement to contributory benefits.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Some low-earning workers, such as part-timers, may not qualify for statutory maternity pay.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Workers with low earnings, such as some part-time staff, may miss out on statutory payments like maternity pay.

items.prompt: What is a National Insurance number?
distractors: A number needed to register a car
A number given to every voter
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): It ensures that the tax and contributions you pay are recorded against your name.

items.prompt: When are young people in the UK sent their National Insurance number?
distractors: When they first register to vote
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Every young person receives a National Insurance number shortly before turning 16.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: You can start work in the UK before you have a National Insurance number.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): You can begin working without one, but you will need one if you work or are self-employed.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, which department should a person with permission to work telephone to arrange a National Insurance number?
items.answer: The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP)
distractors: The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA)
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The handbook says to phone the DWP, which explains the application process and documents needed.
items.notes: changed since publication: applications are now usually made online through gov.uk

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: A National Insurance number on its own proves to an employer that you have the right to work in the UK.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): A National Insurance number by itself is not proof of the right to work.

items.prompt: What is the minimum age to ride a moped in the UK?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): You can ride a moped at 16, while cars and motorcycles require you to be 17.

items.prompt: What is the first step towards driving, according to government guidelines in the handbook?
items.answer: Applying for a provisional driving licence and finding an instructor
distractors: Buying a car and insuring it
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Learners first get a provisional licence and an instructor, then pass theory and practical tests.

items.prompt: The driving theory test is made up of a multiple choice test and which other part?
distractors: An eyesight test at a hospital
A test of vehicle repair skills
A written essay on the Highway Code
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The theory test has a multiple choice section and a hazard perception section.

items.prompt: Up to what age can drivers use their licence before having to renew it every three years?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): A licence lasts until the driver is 70, then is valid for three years at a time.

items.prompt: In Northern Ireland, what must a newly qualified driver display for one year after passing the test?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Newly qualified drivers in Northern Ireland show an 'R' plate for a year.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, for how long can someone use a driving licence from Brazil to drive in the UK?
distractors: As long as the licence is valid
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Licences from countries outside the listed European ones can be used for up to 12 months, after which a UK licence is needed.

items.prompt: Where must a car or motorcycle of a UK resident be registered?
items.answer: The Driver and Vehicle Licensing Agency (DVLA)
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Residents' vehicles must be registered with the DVLA.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, what did drivers display on the windscreen to show that road tax had been paid?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The handbook says vehicle owners pay annual road tax and display a tax disc.
items.notes: changed since publication: paper tax discs were abolished in October 2014

items.prompt: What do the letters MOT in 'MOT test' stand for?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The annual vehicle check is called the Ministry of Transport (MOT) test.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: According to the handbook, people who disregard the law should not expect to be granted permanent residence.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): All residents must obey the law; anyone who disregards it should not expect to be allowed to settle permanently.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: In the UK, the law applies differently to people depending on where they come from.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Everyone receives equal treatment under the law, whoever they are and wherever they come from.

items.prompt: Who usually investigates crimes in the UK?
items.answer: The police, or another body such as a local council
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Crimes are normally investigated by the police or another authority, and then punished by the courts.

items.prompt: What is civil law used for?
items.answer: Settling disputes between individuals or groups
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Civil law deals with disputes between people or groups, while criminal law deals with crimes.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: It is legal to carry a knife in the UK if it is only for self-defence.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Carrying any weapon is a criminal offence, even for self-defence.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Buying or selling cannabis is legal in the UK.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Dealing in or buying drugs including cannabis, heroin, cocaine and ecstasy is against the law.

items.prompt: What is a racial crime under UK law?
items.answer: Harassing, alarming or distressing a person because of their ethnic origin or religion
distractors: Refusing to learn a foreign language
Moving to a different area of the UK
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Targeting someone with harassment, alarm or distress because of their religion or ethnic origin is a crime.

items.prompt: What is the minimum age for buying tobacco products in the UK?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Selling cigarettes, cigars or other tobacco to anyone under 18 is illegal.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: It is illegal to smoke tobacco in almost all enclosed public places in the UK.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Smoking is banned in almost all enclosed public places, and signs show where you cannot smoke.

items.prompt: From what age may someone have an alcoholic drink with a meal in a restaurant or hotel?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): There is an exception to the age-18 rule: those aged 16 and over may have an alcoholic drink with a meal in a restaurant or hotel.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: It is a criminal offence to buy alcohol for someone who is under 18.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Both selling alcohol to under-18s and buying it for them are criminal offences.

items.prompt: What are areas where people are not allowed to drink alcohol in public called?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Some places have alcohol-free zones, and the police can confiscate alcohol.

items.prompt: A dispute between a landlord and a tenant about repairs or eviction falls under which kind of law?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Housing law, covering landlord and tenant disputes, is an example of civil law.

items.prompt: Which area of civil law covers cases of unfair dismissal or disputes over wages?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Employment law deals with wages, unfair dismissal and workplace discrimination.

items.prompt: What does 'keeping the peace' mean as a duty of the police?
distractors: Settling disputes between neighbours in court
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): One of the police's jobs is to prevent disturbances, also called keeping the peace.

items.prompt: Who heads each of the UK's separate police forces?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Police forces are organised separately, each headed by a Chief Constable.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Police forces in the UK are under the direct control of the government.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The separate police forces, each headed by a Chief Constable, are independent of the government.

items.prompt: When did the public first elect Police and Crime Commissioners in England and Wales?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): PCCs were first elected in November 2012.

items.prompt: Who appoints the Chief Constable of a police force in England and Wales?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): PCCs set local priorities and budgets and appoint the Chief Constable.

items.prompt: Which of these must police officers NOT do?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Officers must obey the law and must not misuse authority, lie, be rude or abusive, or discriminate on racial grounds.

items.prompt: If you are arrested and taken to the police station, what happens?
items.answer: An officer tells you why you were arrested and you can seek legal advice
distractors: You lose the right to speak to a lawyer
You are automatically taken to court that day
You must pay a fine before being released
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Arrested people are told the reason for their arrest and may get legal advice.

items.prompt: Which independent body deals with complaints about the police in Northern Ireland?
items.answer: The Police Ombudsman for Northern Ireland
distractors: The Equality Commission for Northern Ireland
The Electoral Office for Northern Ireland
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Complaints in Northern Ireland can go to the Police Ombudsman.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, which independent body handles complaints about the police in England and Wales?
distractors: The Equality and Human Rights Commission
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The handbook names the Independent Police Complaints Commission for England and Wales.
items.notes: changed since publication: replaced by the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) in 2018

items.prompt: According to the handbook, what is the most serious terrorist threat facing the UK?
items.answer: Al Qa'ida, its affiliates and like-minded organisations
distractors: Pirates operating in the English Channel
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The handbook names Al Qa'ida and related groups as the most serious threat, alongside other threats such as Northern Ireland-related terrorism.
items.notes: changed since publication: threat assessments now also highlight other groups (e.g. Islamic State)

items.prompt: How does the handbook define extremism?
items.answer: Active or vocal opposition to fundamental British values
distractors: Voting for a small political party
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The handbook describes extremism as opposing fundamental British values, whether vocally or actively; it covers both religious and far-right forms.

items.prompt: If you believe someone is trying to draw you into an extremist or terrorist cause, what should you do?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): You should notify your local police force.

items.prompt: What is the collective name for judges?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Judges together are called the judiciary; they interpret the law and ensure fair trials.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The government can interfere with the way judges interpret the law and run trials.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Judges interpret the law and ensure fair trials, and the government cannot interfere.

items.prompt: If judges agree that an action of the government is illegal, what must the government do?
items.answer: Change its policies or ask Parliament to change the law
distractors: Hold a referendum on the judgment
Ask the monarch to overturn the ruling
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The government must either alter its policies or ask Parliament for a change in the law.

items.prompt: What can judges order if a public body is not respecting someone's legal rights?
items.answer: That the body changes its practices and/or pays compensation
distractors: That the body's staff are sent to prison
That a General Election is held
That the body is sold to a private company
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Judges may require the body to change how it works and/or to pay compensation.

items.prompt: In Northern Ireland, who hears cases in a Magistrates' Court?
items.answer: A paid, legally qualified District Judge or Deputy District Judge
distractors: Unpaid local volunteers with no legal training
A jury of 12 members of the public
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Unlike England, Wales and Scotland, Northern Ireland uses paid, legally qualified District Judges.

items.prompt: In Scotland, where are serious criminal cases heard?
items.answer: In a Sheriff Court, with a sheriff or a sheriff and jury
distractors: In a Crown Court with a judge and jury
In a Justice of the Peace Court
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Serious Scottish cases go to a Sheriff Court, and the most serious to the High Court.

items.prompt: In Scotland, where are the most serious criminal cases, such as murder, heard?
items.answer: At a High Court with a judge and jury
distractors: At a Justice of the Peace Court
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The most serious Scottish cases are heard by a judge and jury at a High Court.

items.prompt: How are members of a jury chosen?
items.answer: At random from the local electoral register
distractors: By the judge from among local lawyers
By the local council from volunteers
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Jurors are members of the public picked at random from the electoral register.

items.prompt: Which of these could make someone not eligible for jury service?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Everyone summoned must serve unless ineligible, for example due to a criminal conviction, or excused for a good reason like ill health.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, which third verdict, besides 'guilty' and 'not guilty', is possible in Scotland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Scottish juries could also return a verdict of 'not proven'.
items.notes: changed since publication: the Scottish Parliament legislated in 2025 to abolish the 'not proven' verdict

items.prompt: If a jury finds a defendant guilty, who decides the penalty?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The jury decides the verdict and the judge then decides the penalty.

items.prompt: Who normally hears a case in a Youth Court?
items.answer: Up to three specially trained magistrates or a District Judge
distractors: A judge and a jury of 12
A sheriff and a jury of 15
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Youth Court cases are heard by up to three specially trained magistrates or a District Judge.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Members of the public are allowed to watch hearings in a Youth Court.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The public are not allowed in Youth Courts.

items.prompt: Which of these is true of cases in a Youth Court?
items.answer: The accused young person's name and photograph cannot be published by the media
distractors: The case is always heard by a jury
The parents are not allowed to attend
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Media may not publish the name or photographs of the young person, and parents or carers are expected to attend.

items.prompt: In Scotland, which system deals with young people who have committed offences?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Scotland uses the Children's Hearings System for young offenders.

items.prompt: Which system does Northern Ireland use to consider how a child who has committed an offence should be dealt with?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Northern Ireland has a youth conferencing system.

items.prompt: In England and Wales, which courts deal with civil disputes such as divorce, personal injury and recovering money owed?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Many kinds of civil dispute are handled by County Courts.

items.prompt: In Scotland, which court deals with most of the civil matters handled by County Courts elsewhere?
distractors: The Justice of the Peace Court
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Most such civil matters in Scotland go to the Sheriff Court.

items.prompt: In Scotland, where are serious civil cases, such as large compensation claims, dealt with?
items.answer: The Court of Session in Edinburgh
distractors: A Justice of the Peace Court
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Serious civil cases go to the High Court in England, Wales and Northern Ireland and to the Court of Session in Scotland.

items.prompt: In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, where are serious civil cases dealt with?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Serious civil cases, such as those claiming large compensation, go to the High Court.

items.prompt: In England and Wales, the small claims procedure is used for claims of less than what amount?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): In England and Wales small claims are those under £10,000.

items.prompt: Where is a small claims hearing held?
items.answer: In an ordinary room in front of a judge, with both sides sitting around a table
distractors: In a Crown Court in front of a jury
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The hearing is informal, before a judge in an ordinary room.

items.prompt: How can a small claim be issued online?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Small claims can be started online using Money Claims Online.

items.prompt: What do solicitors do?
items.answer: Give legal advice, act for their clients and represent them in court
distractors: Decide verdicts in Crown Court trials
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Solicitors are trained lawyers who advise clients, take action for them and represent them in court.

items.prompt: What are solicitors' charges usually based on?
items.answer: How much time they spend on a case
distractors: A fixed fee set by Parliament
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Charges usually depend on time spent, so check the likely cost at the start.

items.prompt: Which organisation in England and Wales can give you information about solicitors?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The Law Society (and its Scottish and Northern Irish equivalents) and Citizens Advice can help you find a solicitor.

items.prompt: Who is the Prime Minister?
items.answer: The leader of the political party in power
distractors: The longest-serving member of the House of Lords
The person chosen by the Speaker
The head of the civil service
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The PM leads the governing party, appoints the cabinet and controls many public appointments.

items.prompt: How can a Prime Minister be replaced between General Elections?
items.answer: MPs in the governing party decide to change the leader, or the PM resigns
distractors: The House of Lords votes to remove them
The monarch dismisses them after a cabinet complaint
The Speaker calls a public vote
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): A PM can be changed by MPs in the governing party, or if they wish to resign.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: A Prime Minister usually resigns if their party loses a General Election.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): When the governing party loses a General Election, the PM normally resigns.

items.prompt: About how many senior MPs does the Prime Minister appoint as ministers in charge of departments?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The PM appoints around 20 senior MPs to head departments, forming the cabinet.

items.prompt: How often does the cabinet usually meet?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The cabinet is a committee that normally meets every week to decide government policy.

items.prompt: What are the ministers in charge of areas like health, education or defence called?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Ministers in charge of areas like education and health are called Secretaries of State.

items.prompt: Besides cabinet ministers, which other ministers take charge of particular areas of a department's work?
items.answer: Ministers of State and Parliamentary Under-Secretaries of State
distractors: Magistrates and Justices of the Peace
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Each department has further ministers: Ministers of State and Parliamentary Under-Secretaries of State.

items.prompt: What is the role of the shadow cabinet?
items.answer: To challenge the government and propose different policies
distractors: To advise the monarch on royal duties
To run the government when the PM is abroad
To count the votes at General Elections
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Shadow ministers, appointed by the leader of the opposition, challenge the government and suggest alternatives.

items.prompt: What is the minimum age for standing for election as an MP?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Anyone aged 18 or over can stand, though they are unlikely to win without a major party's nomination.

items.prompt: Which TWO are named in the handbook as major political parties?
items.answer: The Conservative Party and the Labour Party
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The major parties named are the Conservatives, Labour, the Liberal Democrats and parties representing Scottish, Welsh or Northern Irish interests.

items.prompt: How often do the main political parties hold policy-making conferences?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The main parties have branches in most constituencies and hold annual policy-making conferences.

items.prompt: Which organisation represents the views of British business?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The CBI is a representative pressure group for British business.

items.prompt: Which pressure group is given in the handbook as an example of campaigning on human rights?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Liberty is named as a human rights campaign group, and Greenpeace as an environmental one.

items.prompt: Greenpeace is given as an example of a pressure group that campaigns on which issue?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Greenpeace campaigns on the environment.

items.prompt: Which of these is one of the core values of the civil service?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The core values are integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality, including political neutrality.

items.prompt: How are civil servants chosen?
items.answer: On merit, through an application process like other jobs
distractors: By the governing party after each election
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Civil servants are selected on merit and are not political appointees.

items.prompt: To whom are civil servants accountable?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Civil servants support the government and are accountable to ministers.

items.prompt: What are the democratically elected councils that govern towns, cities and rural areas often called?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Elected councils are often known as local authorities.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Some areas of the UK have both district and county councils with different functions.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Some areas have two tiers of council, while most large towns and cities have a single authority.

items.prompt: How are local authorities funded?
items.answer: Through central government funding and local taxes
distractors: Only by fines collected by the police
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Councils are funded partly by central government and partly by local taxation.

items.prompt: In many local authorities, what is the role of the mayor?
distractors: Head of the local police force
Member of the House of Lords
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Many councils appoint a mayor as ceremonial leader; in some towns an elected mayor leads the administration.

items.prompt: How many local authorities does London have?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): There are 33 local authorities in London, with policy across the capital coordinated by the Mayor of London and the Greater London Authority.

items.prompt: Since which year have some powers been devolved from central government to Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Devolution of some powers began in 1997.

items.prompt: Which TWO policy areas remain under the control of the central UK government?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Defence, foreign affairs, immigration, taxation and social security stay with the UK government.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland's devolved administrations each have a separate civil service.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Each devolved administration has a civil service of its own.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, how many members does the National Assembly for Wales have?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The handbook gives 60 Assembly Members (AMs) for Wales.
items.notes: changed since publication: renamed the Senedd (Welsh Parliament) in 2020; members are now MSs and the number rises to 96 from the 2026 election

items.prompt: According to the handbook, how often are elections held for the National Assembly for Wales?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): According to the handbook, Welsh Assembly elections were held every four years under a type of proportional representation.
items.notes: changed since publication: Senedd terms are now five years

items.prompt: Which statement about languages in the National Assembly for Wales is correct?
items.answer: Members may speak in Welsh or English, and publications are in both
distractors: Only Welsh may be spoken in debates
Only English may be used for official publications
Members must speak Welsh to be elected
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Members can use either language and all the Assembly's publications are bilingual.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, in how many areas does the Welsh Assembly have power to make laws?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The handbook says the Assembly can legislate in 20 areas, such as education, health and housing.
items.notes: changed since publication: the Wales Act 2017 moved Wales to a reserved-powers model

items.prompt: Which of these is an area in which the National Assembly for Wales can make laws?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The Welsh Assembly's law-making areas include housing, health, education and economic development.

items.prompt: Since which year has the National Assembly for Wales been able to pass laws on its devolved topics without the UK Parliament's agreement?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): From 2011 the Assembly could legislate on these topics without UK Parliament agreement.

items.prompt: How many members does the Scottish Parliament have?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): There are 129 MSPs, elected by a form of proportional representation.

items.prompt: On which matters can the Scottish Parliament pass laws?
items.answer: All matters not specifically reserved to the UK Parliament
distractors: Only matters approved by the House of Lords
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The Scottish Parliament can legislate on anything not reserved to Westminster.

items.prompt: Which of these can the Scottish Parliament legislate on?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Matters for the Scottish Parliament include civil and criminal law, health, education, planning and additional tax-raising powers.

items.prompt: The Northern Ireland Assembly was established soon after which agreement?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The Assembly followed the 1998 Belfast Agreement and shares ministerial offices among the main parties.

items.prompt: What does the power-sharing agreement in the Northern Ireland Assembly do?
items.answer: Distributes ministerial offices among the main parties
distractors: Gives all power to the largest party
Lets the UK Parliament appoint every minister
Shares seats equally with the Irish Parliament
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Ministerial offices are distributed among the main parties under power-sharing.

items.prompt: How many elected members does the Northern Ireland Assembly have?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The Assembly has 90 MLAs elected by a form of proportional representation.

items.prompt: What are members of the Northern Ireland Assembly called?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Northern Ireland Assembly members are known as MLAs.

items.prompt: Which of these is an issue the Northern Ireland Assembly can make decisions on?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The Assembly decides on matters such as education, agriculture, the environment, health and social services.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The UK government can suspend any of the devolved assemblies.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The UK government can suspend devolved assemblies and has done so several times in Northern Ireland.

items.prompt: What does it mean that the UK has a free press?
items.answer: Newspapers are not controlled by the government
distractors: Newspapers are given away free of charge
Newspapers may only report on sport
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): A free press means newspapers are not controlled by the government.

items.prompt: What does the law require of radio and television coverage of political parties?
items.answer: It must be balanced, giving equal time to rival viewpoints
distractors: It must support the governing party
It must be approved by the Prime Minister
It is banned during election campaigns
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Broadcast coverage of parties must by law be balanced.

items.prompt: How can you find out which local authority you come under for voter registration?
items.answer: Visit www.aboutmyvote.co.uk and enter your postcode
distractors: Write to the Speaker of the House
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The aboutmyvote website identifies your local authority from your postcode.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, when is the electoral register updated each year?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The handbook says the register is updated annually in September or October, using a form sent to every household.
items.notes: changed since publication: the annual canvass now runs over the summer and autumn, with the revised register published by 1 December; Great Britain moved to individual registration in 2014

items.prompt: What is the voter registration system used in Northern Ireland called?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): In Northern Ireland every person entitled to vote completes their own form.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Each local authority must, by law, make its electoral register available for anyone to look at, under supervision.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Anyone may inspect the register under supervision at the electoral registration office or some public buildings such as libraries.

items.prompt: What does the poll card you are sent before an election tell you?
items.answer: Where your polling station is and when the election takes place
distractors: Which candidate you must vote for
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The poll card shows the location of your polling station or place and the election date.

items.prompt: During what hours are polling stations open on election day?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Polling stations and places open from 7 am until 10 pm.

items.prompt: What are polling stations called in Scotland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): In Scotland the term used is polling places.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, in which part of the UK must voters also show photographic identification at the polling station?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The handbook states that photo ID is required in Northern Ireland.
items.notes: changed since publication: photo ID has also been required at UK parliamentary and English local elections since 2023

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Nobody is entitled to force you to vote for a certain candidate.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): You fill in your ballot privately and should decide for yourself whom to vote for.

items.prompt: If it is difficult to get to a polling station, how else can you vote?
items.answer: By registering for a postal ballot
distractors: By telephoning the council on election day
By asking a police officer to vote for you
By emailing your vote to your MP
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): With a postal ballot your ballot paper is sent to your home and you post it back.

items.prompt: Which of these groups cannot stand for public office?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Exceptions include members of the armed forces, civil servants and people guilty of certain criminal offences.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Members of the House of Lords may stand for election to the House of Commons.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Peers cannot stand for the House of Commons, though they may stand for every other public office.

items.prompt: Which is usually easier for visitors to get into?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Queues for the Commons can be long, but it is usually easier to get into the Lords.

items.prompt: How can you get tickets to watch debates at the Palace of Westminster?
items.answer: Write to your local MP in advance or queue on the day
distractors: Buy them from a ticket agency
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): You can request tickets from your MP or queue at the public entrance; entry is free.

items.prompt: What is the name of the place in Belfast where the Northern Ireland Assembly meets?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): MLAs meet in the Northern Ireland Assembly at Stormont in Belfast.

items.prompt: Where in Edinburgh is the Scottish Parliament building?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): MSPs meet in the Scottish Parliament building at Holyrood.

items.prompt: In which building do Welsh Assembly members meet?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The Welsh Assembly meets in the Senedd, an open building in Cardiff Bay.

items.prompt: On which core values is the Commonwealth based?
items.answer: Democracy, good government and the rule of law
distractors: Free trade, a single currency and open borders
Military defence and shared armed forces
A common religion and a common language
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Commonwealth members work together on democracy and development, based on democracy, good government and the rule of law.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Commonwealth has the power to suspend a country's membership.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The Commonwealth has no power over its members but can suspend membership.

items.prompt: Who is the ceremonial head of the Commonwealth?
distractors: The Secretary-General of the United Nations
The President of the Council of Europe
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The monarch is the Commonwealth's ceremonial head.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Every member of the Commonwealth was once part of the British Empire.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Most members were once in the British Empire, but a few countries that were not have also joined.

items.prompt: Which of these European countries is a member of the Commonwealth?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The European members listed are Cyprus, Malta and the United Kingdom.

items.prompt: Which of these Asian countries is a member of the Commonwealth?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Asian members include Bangladesh, India, Malaysia, Pakistan, Singapore and Sri Lanka.

items.prompt: What is the Council of Europe responsible for?
items.answer: Protecting and promoting human rights in its member countries
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The Council of Europe, separate from the EU, protects and promotes human rights.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, how many member countries does the Council of Europe have?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The handbook says the Council of Europe has 47 members, including the UK.
items.notes: changed since publication: 46 members since Russia was expelled in 2022

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: The Council of Europe has the power to make laws for its member countries.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): It cannot make laws but draws up conventions and charters, such as the European Convention on Human Rights.

items.prompt: About how many countries are members of the United Nations?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The UN is an international organisation with over 190 member countries.

items.prompt: When was the United Nations set up?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The UN was created after the Second World War to prevent war and promote peace and security.

items.prompt: How many members are there on the UN Security Council?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The Security Council has 15 members, five of them permanent, including the UK.

items.prompt: What does the UN Security Council do?
items.answer: Recommends action during international crises and threats to peace
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The Security Council recommends action when there are crises or threats to peace.

items.prompt: What is NATO?
items.answer: An alliance of European and North American countries pledged to help one another if attacked
distractors: A trade association of former British colonies
A European court of human rights
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): NATO members agree to help one another if attacked and aim to keep peace among themselves.

items.prompt: Which of these is one of the shared values and responsibilities listed for everyone in the UK?
items.answer: To vote in local and national government elections
distractors: To attend a place of worship
To live in the same area for life
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Shared responsibilities include obeying the law, helping others and voting in local and national elections.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Respecting and preserving the environment is listed as one of the shared responsibilities of people in the UK.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Looking after the environment is among the shared values and responsibilities.

items.prompt: What does the handbook suggest you do when you move into a new home?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Getting to know neighbours helps you become part of the community and make friends.

items.prompt: Which of these helps prevent problems with your neighbours?
items.answer: Respecting their privacy and limiting noise
distractors: Leaving rubbish bags on the street at all times
Playing loud music late at night
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Respect neighbours' privacy, keep noise down and keep your garden tidy.

items.prompt: When should rubbish bags and bins be put out on the street?
items.answer: Only when they are due to be collected
distractors: Once a month, on the first day
At any time, day or night
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Bins and rubbish bags should go out only when due for collection.

items.prompt: According to the handbook, people on the electoral register within which age range can be selected for jury service?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The handbook says anyone on the register aged 18 to 70 can be asked to serve on a jury.
items.notes: changed since publication: the upper age limit in England and Wales was raised to 75 in 2016

items.prompt: Which of these is one way parents can help in their children's school?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Parents can help in classrooms, support activities or listen to children read.

items.prompt: What do the letters PTA stand for?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): School events are sometimes organised by parent-teacher associations.

items.prompt: What are school governors called in Scotland?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): In Scotland the equivalent of school governors are members of the school board.

items.prompt: What is the age requirement for becoming a school governor?
items.answer: 18 or over, with no upper age limit
distractors: Any age, if a parent of a pupil
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Governors must be 18 or older when elected or appointed, with no upper age limit.

items.prompt: Which of these is one of the three key roles of school governors?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Governors set the school's strategic direction, ensure accountability and monitor performance.

items.prompt: In England, who may apply to set up a free school locally?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Parents, as well as other community groups, may apply to set up a free school in England.

items.prompt: What is 'canvassing'?
items.answer: Party members asking people for their support, for example by knocking on doors
distractors: Registering people on the electoral roll
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Canvassing means persuading people to vote for a party's candidates, by leafleting or door-knocking.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: You must tell a canvasser how you intend to vote.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): You do not have to tell a canvasser how you will vote if you do not want to.

items.prompt: Which of these is a way to volunteer with the police?
distractors: Becoming a Police and Crime Commissioner
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): You can volunteer as a special constable or a lay (non-police) representative.

items.prompt: Which of these local bodies may advertise for volunteers to serve on their governing bodies?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Universities, housing associations, museums and arts councils may seek volunteers for their governing bodies.

items.prompt: About how long does it take to give blood?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Giving blood takes only around an hour.

items.prompt: How can registering as an organ donor help?
items.answer: It can help your family decide whether to donate your organs after your death
distractors: It gives you priority for NHS treatment
It exempts you from jury service
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Registering helps your family decide on organ donation after your death.

items.prompt: TRUE or FALSE: Living people can donate a kidney.
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Besides donation after death, living people can donate a kidney.

items.prompt: What is volunteering?
items.answer: Working for good causes without payment
distractors: Working for the government on a fixed contract
Doing compulsory community service ordered by a court
Working abroad for an international company
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Volunteering means unpaid work for good causes.

items.prompt: Which of these is given as a benefit of volunteering?
items.answer: A chance to practise English or develop work skills
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Volunteering can help you practise English, gain work skills and improve your CV.

items.prompt: Which of these is given as an example of mentoring as a volunteer?
items.answer: Supporting someone who has just come out of prison
distractors: Caring for animals at a rescue shelter
Working on a hospital information desk
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Mentoring, such as supporting someone recently released from prison, is one volunteering activity.

items.prompt: Which charity works with children?
items.answer: The National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children (NSPCC)
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The NSPCC is given as an example of a charity working with children.

items.prompt: Which charity works with older people?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Age UK is named as a charity working with older people.

items.prompt: Which TWO charities are given as examples of organisations working with homeless people?
distractors: Cancer Research UK and the PDSA
Friends of the Earth and the British Red Cross
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Crisis and Shelter are the examples of charities for the homeless.

items.prompt: What kind of charity is the People's Dispensary for Sick Animals (PDSA)?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The PDSA is named as an animal charity.

items.prompt: Which of these is given as an example of a medical research charity?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Cancer Research UK is the example of a medical research charity.

items.prompt: Which TWO are given as examples of environmental charities?
items.answer: The National Trust and Friends of the Earth
distractors: Cancer Research UK and the PDSA
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Environmental charities named include the National Trust and Friends of the Earth.

items.prompt: The British Red Cross is given as an example of what?
items.answer: A British branch of an international organisation
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Charities range from British branches of international bodies like the Red Cross to small local charities.

items.prompt: Which programme gives 16- and 17-year-olds the chance to do outdoor activities, develop skills and take part in a community project?
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): The National Citizen Service is for young people aged 16 and 17.

items.prompt: Why does using recycled materials to make new products help the environment?
items.answer: It uses less energy and reduces the need to extract raw materials
distractors: It makes products more expensive, so people buy less
It increases the amount of rubbish sent to landfill
It means factories can work longer hours
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Recycling saves energy, means fewer raw materials are taken from the earth and reduces landfill.

items.prompt: Which of these is a benefit of shopping for products locally?
items.answer: It helps local businesses and farmers and reduces your carbon footprint
distractors: It means you pay no VAT
It entitles you to vote in local elections
It increases the amount of packaging used
items.explanation: Handbook ch. 5 (The UK government, the law and your role): Buying locally supports local businesses and farmers and cuts the distance products travel.
